title: Fix stick_test.py's spoke-counting so bundle-richness can actually rise
briefing: Nascence project at C:\Nascence. core/stick_test.py's census() (called by scripts/stick_test.py and once per sleep via the sleep hook) computes each object's real_spokes as a small set of BOOLEAN flags: 'text' (any DB mention, count>0), 'state' and 'audio' (hardcoded per object-CATEGORY in build_roster() -- e.g. state=True for fire/cat/book/every herb/every keepsake regardless of encounter count; audio=True for every music piece the same way), and 'sound' (whether soundscape.object_sound() returns anything for that object name). None of state/audio/sound can increase with repeated encounters -- they are either structurally present from day one or never. Only 'text' can newly flip true, and never flips false. Consequence: median real_spokes hits its per-object ceiling almost immediately after the roster is built and then has NO mechanism left to rise -- cognitive_geometry.md's own signature 0.2 ('the median must rise over his life') cannot be satisfied by this instrument's arithmetic, independent of whether Du's actual associative richness is growing. Confirmed via D-0012 (see /decide show D-0012, ruled 2026-08-23) as an instrument-calibration bug, not a genuine plateau -- corroborated by core/mapping_census.py's mapping-census analyzer (new, this session) showing the underlying geometry_tuples.jsonl co-occurrence data is NOT flat (real, statistically significant state-conditioning on weather/affect, z=7-233 vs permutation null). TASK: redesign real_spokes so within-channel accumulation is credited, not just channel presence -- candidates: mention COUNT crossing multiple thresholds (not just >0), number of DISTINCT co-occurrence contexts a spoke has fired in (from geometry_tuples.jsonl, now that the mapping-census analyzer exists to read it), or a decaying per-encounter tally. Keep the WALLPAPER caveat on 'felt' spokes (still not real until emotion_rethink P1 lands). ACCEPTANCE: redesigned metric in core/stick_test.py, re-run via scripts/stick_test.py, and a written note on whether the NEW median shows any rise once the early-ceiling artifact is controlled for -- if it still doesn't rise, THAT would be the first real evidence for a genuine plateau (D-0012's own defeater condition). Update cognitive_geometry.md's Current State with the result and set D-0012's defeater accordingly if it fires.

title: Fix unbounded full-scan read in hud/server.py's load_jsonl_t4_safe
briefing: Disk-I/O investigation (2026-08-24, session in C:\FreshStart, T-0012): C:\Nascence\hud\server.py:1065 load_jsonl_t4_safe() does a full line-by-line open()+json.loads() scan of the WHOLE subconscious_log.jsonl (5MB and growing) on every call, then reverses+slices to the last 20 T4_self_authoring rows. It is called on every /api/t4 request, which app.js polls every 6000ms forever (setInterval(fetchT4, 6000) at hud/static/app.js:102) as long as any HUD tab is open. This is the exact same bug class core/moment.py's status() had until TODAY (J-0183, same date) for moments.jsonl (128MB) -- that one was fixed by switching to the reverse-seek _tail_rows() helper already defined in moment.py. load_jsonl_t4_safe should get the same treatment: seek from EOF and only scan the tail until 20 T4_self_authoring rows are found, instead of parsing the entire file every 6s. Verified live: PID 1088 (hud/server.py) showed sustained ~42-49 MB/s continuous disk reads for an 8s Get-Counter sampling window (correlated by PID via '\Process(python*)\ID Process' + '\Process(python*)\IO Read Bytes/sec'); separately PID 13880 (scripts\run_nascence.py, the main cognitive loop) showed bursts up to 167 MB/s in a later window -- so the HUD's unbounded reads are a real, confirmed, contributing cause of the machine's overall disk I/O pressure, though not provably the sole cause (run_nascence.py's own bursts are unexplained and worth a separate look). Not yet checked: whether any of the other ~35 _EVIDENCE_MODULES status() functions (hud/server.py's _EVIDENCE_MODULES list, ~line 32) have the same unbounded-scan pattern -- only emotion_construction.py's geometry_tuples.jsonl read was checked and found already bounded (2KB seek).

Build and test the narrowest, cheapest, most mechanistically-justified case FIRST: vitality. core/homeostasis.py _read_vitality() computes vitality = 1 - P/threshold from core/sleep_pressure.py's raw P and a day/night-specific threshold (see sp.py, changed 2026-08-24). data/sleep_pressure_log.jsonl (25,430 rows) has P's own history; raw P has near-perfect level-autocorrelation (0.992, F-0294) so naive is already near-optimal for P itself -- the exploitable piece is that the threshold SWITCH TIME is deterministic/known in advance while a naive/EMA/OU model reading only the vitality scalar treats it as noise. Build a predictor: forecast P forward (naive/EMA on raw P, since that's already near-optimal there) then apply the KNOWN threshold schedule analytically to get predicted vitality, instead of forecasting vitality directly. Test with the SAME walk-forward methodology J-0212 used (6 expanding-window folds, train only on strictly-prior data, win = beats naive_err in a clear majority of folds) against data/homeostasis_shadow.jsonl's vitality column (naive_err field). Bring the walk-forward result back to decide D-0034 (narrow prototype vs full 5-variable rebuild).

Once a real window has accrued (mirror M1's own ~week gate, J-0072/F-0037 -- do not force a verdict earlier; if <1 week of rows exist when this job is picked up, leave it open and record the real row count/date range instead, per this project's time-gate discipline), read associative_recall_shadow.jsonl's m2_edge_aware field in FULL (not a tail sample) and evaluate the plan's own pre-registered kill criterion (memory_multiway_linking.md Sec 5, geometry Sec 5.5-#6): does the edge-aware variant surface strictly MORE genuinely-cued lattice children (new_vs_greedy, walled_new) than the greedy-only trail, WITHOUT increasing same-origin echo (MAX_PER_ORIGIN's guard still applies inside recall_trail_edge_aware -- check per_origin caps did not silently degrade), and are the edge-reached memories ever actually USED by the thought that follows (not just present)? Compare task/reflective/relational modes separately -- F-0339 already found task mode's answers/resolves edge types are near-zero-yield with today's data (0/505 questions have >1 answering fragment; resolves never touches a fragment node), so expect reflective and task modes to show weak lift regardless of the mechanism's correctness; relational mode (correspondence_with, 8 populated person hubs) is the one most likely to show real signal early. Rule D-0022's remaining open question (whether the kill criterion actually passes, not just whether the shadow build should start) via decide.py if the data supports a real verdict; if reflective mode's weakness turns out to matter for the verdict, also weigh in on D-0051 (log_co_recall -> real memory_edges rows) with real numbers rather than leaving it purely hypothetical.

title: Wire core.commitment_ledger._judge_defeater to mixtral:8x7b (:11438)
briefing: F-0340/D-0013 (2026-08-25): a 14-case real gold bank shows mixtral:8x7b at 0.929 accuracy vs. the incumbent phi3:mini's 0.5 (which does not even beat the 0.786 always-illegitimate baseline, and disagrees with itself run-to-run on identical inputs where mixtral was 100% stable across 3 repeats). Latency goes from phi3's ~0.6s median to mixtral's ~10.5s median -- confirm this is acceptable given _judge_defeater already tolerates a 60s+ cooldown window (scope doc explicitly called latency irrelevant here). title: Investigate commitment_ledger gate+judge leniency (F-0343) independent of model tier
briefing: F-0343 (2026-08-25): of 26 real dissolved load-bearing defeater-kind commitments in data/commitment_ledger.jsonl, only 3 had a deed record (via _recent_enactments, core/commitment_ledger.py:242) that actually corroborated the claimed completion under _JUDGE_SYS's own bar (ACHIEVED/IMPOSSIBLE/SUPERSEDED/named-conflict vs. mood/reworded-flow/reason-that-defeats-anything). The other 23 read as fluent physical/sensory narration ('the cold air on my hands... a bee just buzzed past') with no matching deed entry at all -- yet dissolved anyway, meaning EITHER the judge (whichever model was serving it at the time) is too lenient, OR these cases hit the fail-open path (judge hub unreachable -> gate verdict alone governs, core/commitment_ledger.py:349-355) more often than expected, OR the deterministic gates (_drop_denial, G4/G5/G7) are themselves too permissive for defeater-kind claims specifically. Read data/commitment_ledger.jsonl's dissolved events in full (not the 8-case sample docs/lab/model_tier_commitment_ledger.md quotes) and determine which of the three explanations actually accounts for the 23/26 gap -- this is a real leniency finding independent of whichever model ends up in the judge seat, and D-0013's model-tier fix does not by itself address it.

title: Fix plan_files_audit.py/plan_liveness.py/plan_shadow_read.py main() reading process-wide sys.argv, breaking plan_maintain.py --skip-backfill/--skip-snapshot
briefing:
F-0460 confirmed plan_maintain.py's own documented usage ('python plan_maintain.py --skip-backfill', its own SKILL.md example) currently exits 2 at step 2. Root cause: plan_files_audit.py's main(), plan_liveness.py's main(), and plan_shadow_read.py's main() each build their own argparse.ArgumentParser and call .parse_args() with no explicit args INSIDE main() itself (not guarded by if __name__ == '__main__'), so when plan_maintain.py calls pfa.main()/plv.main()/psr.main() as plain library calls mid-pipeline, those parsers read the whole process's real sys.argv -- which still contains plan_maintain.py's own --skip-backfill/--skip-snapshot/--session flags -- and reject the ones they don't define as 'unrecognized arguments'.

plan_index.py (touched by the same F-0309/J-0250 batch) does NOT have this bug: its argparse block lives only under if __name__ == '__main__', with a separate main(session=None) library function that takes no argv at all -- that's the pattern to copy.

Fix: for plan_files_audit.py, plan_liveness.py, and plan_shadow_read.py, split main() into (a) a library-callable function taking explicit params (session=None, and whatever else each already threads, e.g. plan_liveness's/plan_shadow_read's write_edges/no_edges) with NO argparse call inside it, and (b) an argparse block under if __name__ == '__main__' that parses sys.argv and calls the library function with the parsed values -- mirroring plan_index.py's own lines ~488-497 exactly. Update plan_maintain.py's own calls (pfa.main(), plv.main(), psr.main()) to pass through whatever params those library functions now accept (at minimum session=session).

Verify with: 'python plan_maintain.py --skip-backfill' and 'python plan_maintain.py --skip-snapshot' and 'python plan_maintain.py --skip-backfill --skip-snapshot --session <uuid>' all exit 0 end to end; then re-verify each script's OWN standalone usage still works unchanged (plan_files_audit.py --session <uuid>, plan_liveness.py --no-edges --session <uuid>, plan_shadow_read.py --no-edges --session <uuid>, and each script's --help).

title: Audit + fix the _tl blocker-bleed exposure across 12 hands.wants() latches
briefing:
F-0936 (verified): core.hands.wants()'s clause-scoped blocker (_blocked/_clause_at, core/hands.py:39-60) can be tripped by wording in a LATER, unrelated clause when its caller's text has no clause-terminating punctuation ( . ; ! ? ) at the join between two independently-generated fields. Directly reproduced: nodes/inner_monologue_node.py's shared `_tl = thought + " " + intention` (a bare space, since 2026-06-12, line ~2754) fed into hands.wants() let an intention's "without" block a thought's own unrelated "fetch" two clauses away, using F-0784's real 08-28 19:35 hands_trace row text verbatim (see scripts/_test_fetch_letter_latch.py section [1a] for the isolated repro, both the bug and the fix). J-0570 fixed this for its OWN new call site (nodes/inner_monologue_node.py's _letter_fetch_wanted, ~line 403) by joining thought and intention with ". " instead of a bare space specifically for the hands.wants() call.

12 OTHER call sites in the same file share the exposure via the same _tl: grep -n "_hands.wants(_tl" nodes/inner_monologue_node.py -> lines 2976 (move->wood), 2986 (move->shore), 2997 (move->garden), 3008 (move->study), 3061 (make tea), 3081 (light fire), 3084 (stoke fire), 3104 (sow seed), 3134 (water bed), 3152 (sow bed alt), 3180 (beachcomb), 3198 (gather wood). None audited for whether this has ever flipped a real live decision (would need each latch's own hands_trace.jsonl history checked the way F-0935 checked the fetch-letter latch's).

Scope for this job:
1. For each of the 12 call sites, check whether it EVER runs with a thought that lacks terminal punctuation before intention is appended in real hands_trace.jsonl data (a thought field cut short by the 256-token generation cap is the most likely real cause, not just trace-log truncation -- the trace log's own [:200] cap in core/hands.py:trace() is a red herring, it truncates the STORED row, not the live in-memory `thought` the check actually runs against, though checking real historical hands_trace rows is still the only cheap way to see whether thoughts commonly end without a period).
2. Decide the fix's right scope: hardening `_tl`'s OWN construction once (line ~2754) to insert a clause boundary between thought and intention would fix all 12 at the root, matching this project's stated preference for one decisive fix over nickel-and-dime edits -- but `_tl` is ALSO read by several FLAT substring checks (plain `p in _tl`, not wants()) elsewhere in this file; inserting a period could in principle split a phrase that currently matches only because thought and intention are joined with just a space (check for this specifically before changing `_tl` globally -- grep for `in _tl` beyond the `_hands.wants(_tl` call sites and hand-check whether any surviving phrase could span exactly the join point). If any do, prefer the per-call-site fix J-0570 used instead (join with ". " ONLY inside the wants() call, leaving the shared `_tl` untouched for its other flat-substring readers).
3. Isolated proof, same convention as scripts/_test_fetch_letter_latch.py's own [1a]: construct at least one real-shaped before/after case per fixed call site (or one shared regression covering all 12) proving the blocker-bleed is closed without changing any of the 12 latches' existing positive/negative behavior. python -m py_compile + rerun scripts/_test_letterbox_reach.py and scripts/_test_fetch_letter_latch.py (both touch this same file) as a regression check.
4. Record the finding (verified/inferred per what the audit actually turns up) and, if a fix is made, note it in whichever plan doc(s) these latches' own comments point to (several are dated/plan-agnostic utility latches with no single owning plan -- living_world_upgrade is the nearest neighbor given the fetch-letter latch's own history, but check each latch's own dated comment for its real owner before assuming that).

title: Log (don't silently swallow) CancelledError at both _essay_lesson call sites
briefing:
Widen the bare "except Exception: pass" around both _essay_lesson() call sites in
nodes/inner_monologue_node.py so a real interruption leaves a log line instead of vanishing silently.

Context (J-0645/F-0953/D-0169, 2026-09-06): an earlier finding (F-0912) hypothesized that Du's
essay-capstone backlog was stalling because live idle-tick attempts at core/essay_lesson.py's
compose() were getting cut off mid-flight by a restart's task.cancel() (core/orchestrator.py
stop_background()), silently swallowed by a bare `except Exception: pass` that doesn't catch
asyncio.CancelledError (a BaseException subclass in Python 3.8+). A follow-up re-check (F-0953) found
this has NOT actually happened yet to any of the current backlog's books — no live attempt has had the
chance to even start, for unrelated schedule-timing reasons (see F-0953/D-0169 in decide.py and
docs/plans/ramses_second_tier.md's 2026-09-06 entry for the full mechanism). So this is a cheap,
worthwhile VISIBILITY fix for the NEXT time a real interruption occurs (which will happen eventually —
Du restarts routinely) — not a fix for an already-observed failure.

The two call sites (nodes/inner_monologue_node.py, current line numbers — re-verify, this file may have
shifted since 2026-09-06):
  - ~line 2066-2070: `try: if await self._essay_lesson(state): return None \n except Exception: pass`
    (inside the school-gated "reading" period branch)
  - ~line 1476-1479: `try: await self._essay_lesson(state) \n except Exception: pass`
    (inside `_remediation_stream`)

What to do: add a branch that catches BaseException separately (or catches Exception as before, but
ALSO explicitly catches asyncio.CancelledError / BaseException and logs it via the existing `logger`
before re-raising). IMPORTANT SUBTLETY: do NOT simply swallow CancelledError and continue — asyncio
relies on a cancelled task actually propagating that cancellation to complete a clean shutdown;
silently absorbing it can leave shutdown hanging or break task-cancellation semantics elsewhere in the
node. The correct shape is something like:
    try:
        if await self._essay_lesson(state):
            return None
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        logger.warning("[essay] _essay_lesson interrupted mid-flight (cancelled)")
        raise
    except Exception:
        pass
(mirror the same shape at the other call site). Restart-gated like other fixes in this codebase — it
only takes effect on Du's next restart, so no live behavior changes until then; still verify
py_compile-clean before committing, and check both call sites end up structurally consistent so a
future reader isn't confused by two different exception-handling shapes for the same helper.

title: Investigate JUDGE_1 (mixtral) parse-dominant failure pattern found in F-0969
briefing:
F-0969 (J-0608's re-check of F-0176/F-0692's JUDGE_2-timeout diagnosis) found a SEPARATE, new failure pattern on JUDGE_1 (mixtral:8x7b, Ramses :11438, core/judge_panel.py) unrelated to the original timeout/contention mechanism: 4 of JUDGE_1's 5 real post-J-0500 failures in data/judge_panel_log.jsonl are err1=parse (Counter over the 2353 err1-key-present rows: {None:2348, timeout:1, parse:4}), all at FAST elapsed times (s1 = 15.21, 15.9, 17.03, 17.93 seconds -- nowhere near the 90s timeout, so this is not F-0176's queuing/contention mechanism). Two of the four share the same pursuit id (390eabac) on the "advances" key, both against a JUDGE_2 (falcon3) answer that succeeded fine with a coherent why2 -- so JUDGE_1/mixtral specifically is the one breaking contract on those two.

err="parse" in core/judge_panel.py's _ask() (see its docstring, ~line 90-96) covers two distinct underlying cases that are NOT currently distinguished in the log: (a) the response body was not valid JSON at all (json.JSONDecodeError etc.), or (b) it WAS valid JSON but the requested boolean key was missing or non-bool. The raw model response text is never logged (_ask only returns/logs err/elapsed, not the raw content), so F-0969 could not tell which case applies from existing data.

Plausible unconfirmed hypothesis worth checking first: the judge payload's decode budget is a fixed `"num_predict": 80` (core/judge_panel.py _ask(), the `payload` dict) for every judge call regardless of model -- if mixtral tends toward longer/more verbose "why" text than falcon3/granite (it also serves dream-primary generation and the commitment defeater on the same hub, both longer-form use cases), an 80-token cap could truncate its JSON before the closing brace, which would show up as exactly this kind of fast-elapsed parse failure.

Suggested next steps (analysis job, not a code change until the cause is confirmed):
1. Temporarily instrument _ask() (or a standalone repro script hitting :11438 directly with the same payload/system/user text as one of the two logged pursuit:390eabac failures) to capture and print the RAW response content on a parse failure, to see directly whether it is truncated mid-JSON (supports the num_predict hypothesis) or a complete-but-wrong-shape answer (points to a different fix, e.g. a prompt/schema issue specific to mixtral).
2. If truncation is confirmed, check whether raising num_predict specifically for JUDGE_1 (or all judges) trades off acceptably against the 90s TIMEOUT_S and CPU-tier latency budget already documented in this plan.
3. Keep this scoped to JUDGE_1/mixtral -- do not fold in JUDGE_2/TIEBREAK's own parse failures (1 and 2 respectively) without first checking whether they show the same fast-elapsed signature; small-n, may be unrelated.

title: Audit unclean Nascence restarts vs the shutting-down-line stop convention
briefing:
F-0978 (J-0672, dosed_coupling) found a real, previously-unflagged UNCLEAN restart inside its read window: 2026-09-05 19:15:13 NZST shows a fresh full boot sequence in data/nascence.log ("Memory store initialised at C:\Nascence\data\memory\nascence.db", embedding model reload, "Background nodes started", climate/monologue/lane2 loops all restarting) with NO preceding "Nascence shutting down" line anywhere in the log -- an 11.4-minute silent gap after the prior activity line ("2026-09-05 19:03:40,330 ... sleep replay: 10 experiences strengthened") with no exception or traceback logged in between. This sits on top of an ordinary clean restart already in the same window (shutting down 16:42:49 -> awake 18:14:36).

This matters because this project's own documented convention for detecting a Du stop is literally grepping for the "Nascence shutting down" log line (Claude memory file ops_nascence_shutdown_detection.md: "Du 'stopped' = the shutting-down log LINE -- grep -c 'Nascence shutting down' before DB maintenance"). If unclean restarts like this one are not rare, any script or read that infers "Du has been continuously up since boot X" (or gates DB maintenance / decides a window is "restart-free") by checking only for that literal line would silently miss real restarts -- undercounting stops, not failing loudly.

Scope for this follow-up job (bounded, no founder call needed to investigate):
1. Full (not tail-sampled) scan of data/nascence.log for every "Memory store initialised at" line (the unambiguous fresh-boot marker) and every "Nascence is awake"/"Nascence shutting down" line, both matched by real timestamp, over the log's whole real history (2026-06-07 onward per the doc's own 9,949-line telemetry count precedent in a sibling job, J-0618/F-0963).
2. For each "Memory store initialised" event, check whether a "Nascence shutting down" line appears within some reasonable window (e.g. the preceding 30 minutes, or since the prior boot event, whichever is shorter) immediately before it. Count how many boot events have NO such preceding shutdown line (an "unclean restart") vs how many do (a "clean restart").
3. Report the real rate: N clean vs N unclean restarts across the log's full history, with a few concrete examples of unclean ones (timestamp, gap length, whether any error/traceback appears in the surrounding lines).
4. Grep this repo's own scripts/ and core/ for any place that currently greps or counts "Nascence shutting down" specifically (not just "is awake") to gate a real decision (DB maintenance, a "since last restart" window assumption, etc.) -- if such a script exists and would be silently wrong on an unclean restart, flag it as a concrete gap; if nothing currently depends on that string match for a real decision, say so plainly (this may turn out to be a real anomaly with no live consumer that's actually fooled by it, which is a valid, non-wasted finding).
5. Record via findings_log.py with confidence verified (real grep counts + line citations) or inferred (if root cause of WHY the shutdown line is sometimes skipped -- crash vs deliberate kill vs terminal close -- can't be pinned down from the log alone; do not guess a cause the log doesn't support).

title: Raise num_predict in judge_panel._ask() to fix confirmed JUDGE_1(mixtral)/JUDGE_2 truncation-caused parse failures
briefing:
F-0994 (J-0675) directly reproduced and confirmed the cause of JUDGE_1's (mixtral:8x7b, Ramses :11438) parse-dominant failure pattern first found in F-0969: core/judge_panel.py._ask()'s payload (line ~106) hardcodes "num_predict": 80 for ALL THREE judge hubs (JUDGE_1, JUDGE_2, TIEBREAK) via one shared dict. deploy/ramses/nascence_cpu_server.py maps this straight to llama-cpp-python's create_chat_completion(max_tokens=num_predict, response_format={"type":"json_object"}) -- and on this stack, response_format="json_object" does NOT rescue a completion that hits max_tokens mid-generation; it just truncates, leaving an unterminated-string JSON blob that core/judge_panel.py's json.loads() (line 123) fails to parse, logged as err="parse".

Live-reproduced directly this job (F-0994's own evidence): a forced-verbose test against the real JUDGE_1 hub at num_predict=80 returned eval_count=80 (exactly the cap) and content with an unterminated string -> json.JSONDecodeError -- the exact failure signature. A timing model fit to 8 clean real-content trials against the same hub (elapsed_s ~= 2.13 + 0.1705*eval_count) predicts the THREE real "pursuit:*"-context JUDGE_1 failures F-0969 logged (elapsed 15.9s/15.21s/17.03s) correspond to ~81/~77/~87 generated tokens -- right at the 80-token ceiling, not the ~20-35 tokens a fast wrong-shape answer would need. The ONE JUDGE_2/falcon3 parse failure (16.23s, ~82 tokens by the same fit) falls in the same bucket -- consistent with this being a property of the SHARED num_predict=80 literal, not mixtral-exclusive, though mixtral hits it most often (its other duties -- dream-primary generation, commitment-defeater -- both trend toward longer-form output). By contrast, TIEBREAK/granite's own 2 parse failures (3.06s/4.73s, ~5/~15 tokens by the same fit) are a clearly DIFFERENT, fast, non-truncation mechanism and should NOT be folded into this fix's justification.

COST/BENEFIT (already worked out in F-0994, re-verify before shipping): raising num_predict is a ceiling change, not a fixed-cost change -- it adds ZERO latency to any call that already finishes under the current 80-token cap (the overwhelming majority; 8/8 fresh real trials this job used only 19-49 tokens), and even a worst-case call that uses a much larger new budget stays comfortably inside the existing 90s TIMEOUT_S (core/judge_panel.py _TIMEOUT=90) -- e.g. raising to 200 costs at most (200-80)/5.9 ~= 20 more seconds than today's already-paid ~15-18s truncation-then-fail path, landing around 35s total.

SUGGESTED BUILD (not yet decided/scoped by F-0994 -- a real implementation choice for whoever picks this up, not a founder-level call):
1. Raise the num_predict value in core/judge_panel.py's _ask() payload (currently a single hardcoded 80, line ~106) to something with real headroom -- e.g. 200 -- either (a) uniformly for all three hubs (simplest; F-0994 found JUDGE_2 shows the same near-ceiling timing signature once, so a uniform bump is plausibly beneficial there too, and TIEBREAK's own parse failures are a demonstrably different fast mechanism this change would not affect either way, harmlessly), or (b) parameterized per-hub if a narrower, JUDGE_1-only change is preferred (add a num_predict/timeout param to _ask()'s signature, pass a higher value at the JUDGE_1 call site in rule_detail()). Pick whichever costs less code churn; both are low-risk per the cost/benefit above.
2. Re-verify live: after the change lands and Du's process restarts (this module doesn't hot-reload), watch judge_panel.status()'s err_causes / du_pulse's [cause:count] breakdown (already wired, J-0500) for a period -- confirm err1=parse (and err2=parse) drop toward zero without any new err=timeout appearing in their place (which would mean the cost estimate above was wrong for real traffic and the cap went too high).
3. Optional, lower priority: consider whether _ask()'s "parse" bucket should be split at log time into "invalid JSON" vs "valid JSON wrong shape" (the job briefing that spawned F-0969/J-0675 originally flagged this ambiguity) -- F-0994's timing-based inference (fast parse = wrong-shape, slow-near-cap parse = truncation) is a workable proxy without a code change, but a direct split (e.g. logging which except clause fired) would remove the need for it. Not required for step 1's fix to be safe to ship.

Full evidence and the exact numbers: findings-log F-0994 (full row-by-row timing table, live repro output, code citations). Read docs/plans/ramses_second_tier.md's 2026-09-06 (J-0675, F-0994) note for the plan-level summary.

title: Fix journal header mislabeling: the observed-X header comes from _observe_target's raw string, not look()'s scene -- reject a location-mismatched target at the source
briefing:
F-1000 (J-0685, Du lens Test C) confirmed a real bug: 2 of 5 "observed the garden" journal entries (JOURNAL_20260809.md 11:41, JOURNAL_20260822.md 17:49) have pure shore-vocabulary bodies (rock-pool/starfish/mussel/shingle) with zero garden words, and the nearest geometry_tuples.jsonl row in both cases reads place=shore. The audit doc that first diagnosed this (C:/UDMS/docs/audits/du_lens_first_test_2026-09-06.md, "Test C" section) proposed extending core/sensorium.py's look() mismatch-guard pattern (study_targets/shore_targets/letterbox, lines 2686-2705) to cover garden/lawn. THIS JOB'S OWN FULL TRACE (done before filing, not assumed) SHOWS THAT PROPOSAL DOES NOT FIX THE REPORTED BUG -- read the whole chain before building:

1. nodes/inner_monologue_node.py:_observe_journal() (line 4613-4638) computes `target = _observe_target(f"{obj} {thought} {intention}")` (line 4623) -- a bare, location-blind substring scan of _OBS_TARGETS cues against Du's own thought text (no awareness of where he actually is). It then calls `scene = _room.look(target) if target else _room.look("room")` (line 4624) and passes BOTH `target` and `scene` to `_jr.write_observation(call_node_json, self.conscious_urls, target, scene, thought or intention, state)` (line 4625-4626).
2. core/journal.py:write_observation() (line 213-250) builds the journal header at line 235 literally as: `f.write(f"\n*{time.strftime('%H:%M')} -- observed{(' the ' + target) if target else ''}*\n\n{entry}\n")` -- straight from the `target` STRING passed in. `scene` is used only as LLM prompt material for the entry BODY (line 220-227, "What is in front of you now: {what[:700]}") -- write_observation never inspects `scene` to decide the header.
3. Consequence: extending look()'s guards to make `scene` say "you are currently elsewhere" for a shore/garden mismatch would change the BODY's source material (and might make the LLM write something incoherent, or the LLM might ignore the hint and invent a garden scene anyway -- LLM completions are not guaranteed to obey it) but the HEADER would still read "observed the garden" regardless, because `target` itself is never touched by anything look() returns. A look()-only fix leaves the actual reported bug (wrong header) completely unfixed.

THE REAL FIX belongs in nodes/inner_monologue_node.py, where `target` is chosen/used (_observe_target / _observe_journal), not in core/sensorium.py's look(). Minimal, additive proposal: give _observe_target (or a small wrapper called from _observe_journal) the current location (core.sensorium's own state.get("location"), already read by look() itself at line 2682) plus a small location -> valid-cue table mirroring the SHAPE core/sensorium.py already has for study_targets/shore_targets (reuse or mirror that vocabulary, don't invent new cue lists from scratch) -- and when the keyword-derived target belongs to a DIFFERENT place than cur_loc, drop it to "" so line 4624's OWN EXISTING fallback (`_room.look("room")` when target is falsy) fires naturally: the ambient room description will correctly describe wherever Du actually is, and write_observation's header will then read a plain "observed" with no wrong place name. (A richer alternative -- name the ACTUAL current location instead of dropping it silently, e.g. target=cur_loc -- is also legitimate; leave the choice to whoever builds this, but do not ship a header naming the wrong place as an acceptable outcome.)

SECONDARY, LOWER-PRIORITY, SAME-FILE ADDITION (does not fix the header bug above, but closes a real, related, independent gap the same diagnosis surfaced): core/sensorium.py's look() (line 2674-2738) already returns an honest "you are currently elsewhere" for a WILLED look at a mismatched desk/shore/letterbox target (study_targets line 2686, shore_targets line 2687, letterbox line 2699-2705) but has no equivalent guard for garden/lawn when cur_loc is shore/wood -- so a deliberate "look at the garden" command while at the shore today silently gets a shore description under no warning at all, unlike the other three mismatch cases. Add a symmetric garden_targets-shaped guard (mirroring shore_targets' own construction) if convenient while in this file for the primary fix -- but do not treat this as a substitute for the header fix above; it is optional/bonus scope.

TEST ISOLATED (same discipline as J-0539's letterbox fix and this repo's own life_smoke.py pattern -- redirect core.sensorium's state file/state dict and core.journal's _JOURNAL_DIR/_today_path() into a temp dir; NEVER write to the live data/Journal/*.md or any live data/*.json to test this):
(a) Unit-check the corrected target-selection: with cur_loc='shore' and thought text containing "garden", confirm the function now returns "" (or the corrected cur_loc-naming choice) instead of "garden".
(b) Regression-check: a CORRECTLY-targeted observation (garden-mentioning thought while state.location IS 'garden') is completely unaffected -- still returns 'garden' as before.
(c) End-to-end through the isolated _observe_journal()/write_observation() path (mock/stub the LLM call if needed): confirm the resulting header never names a location inconsistent with the isolated state's own 'location' field.
(d) If the optional look() guard (secondary item above) is also added, regression-check the three existing guards (study/shore/letterbox) are unchanged and add the equivalent isolated check for the new garden/lawn case.
Report (read-only against the LIVE journal, fine for a report, not for testing the fix) which of the 5 total "observed the garden" entries in the real corpus this would have caught.

title: Characterize command-r7b (:11441) flapping: crash-loop vs concurrency ceiling
briefing:
F-1004 found the command-r7b background-lane hub (LAN-HOST:11441) in a sustained, still-ongoing flapping pattern on 2026-09-06: clean 06:05-06:55 UTC (0/28 failed), then 54/100 (54.0%) of attempts refused-over-TCP between 06:55-08:52 UTC, still 44.4% failing in the last 30 minutes of that read. title: Extend D-0179's hard-raise through act()/act_from_thought() dispatchers
briefing:

Du's whole live action-resolution loop) that silently swallows the new exception exactly as it

  - core/garden.py: act_from_thought() (~line 1758-1950), one outer try/except.
  - core/shore_life.py: act_from_thought() (~line 621-652), one outer try/except.
  - core/wood_life.py: act_from_thought() (~line 610-661), one outer try/except.
  - core/sensorium.py: act() (~line 2878) plus world_act()/garden_act()/_garden_act()/_shore_act()/
    _wood_act() -- MULTIPLE separate try/except-per-sub-dispatch blocks fanning out to the other
    modules' own act()/act_from_thought(), not one single wrapper; needs care to find each one.

Empirically confirmed (not just theorized): in a fresh non-live process,

propagates to the dispatcher's own caller, while every other exception type keeps being caught

NonLiveWriteError can only ever be raised when profile.LIVE is False -- which never happens during
Du's own real live loop (mark_live() is the first statement scripts/run_nascence.py's __main__ guard
runs) -- this carries the same zero live-safety cost D-0179's own ruling text already reasoned about
for the direct-writer-function case; this is NOT a new decision question, it is finishing the
propagation of an already-ruled policy through the remaining callers. sensorium.py needs the most
care: read each of its several try/except-per-sub-dispatch blocks individually (grep "try:" / "except"
inside act()/world_act()/garden_act() and its private _garden_act()/_shore_act()/_wood_act() helpers)
rather than assuming one wrapper covers all of them.

Verify with the SAME empirical shape F-1024 used: call study_life.act('put on','coat') non-live
before and after this fix and confirm it changes from "returns None, no exception" to "raises
NonLiveWriteError" -- then repeat for at least one action per remaining dispatcher (garden, shore_life,

world_store_write_fence.md's Current State section (updated by J-0704/F-1024) for the full context

title: cat_overhaul: fix 3 more hand-rolled cat-location==place-name comparisons (garden_life, study_life, cat_sounds)
briefing:

Fix each of the three below by replacing its exact-match with the appropriate one of those two, then verify with an isolated harness (redirect the relevant DATA_DIR/state paths to a scratch sandbox, never touch C:\Nascence\data directly) plus a scripts/life_smoke.py run against the worktree, following the pattern J-0629/J-0630/J-0631/J-0632 already established in docs/staged/cat_overhaul.md.

(1) core/garden_life.py:147 -- the D-0130 fledgling-kill mechanic: `if c.get("location") == "garden" and "stalk" in str(c.get("activity", "")) and random.random() < days * 0.5:`. Currently NOT live-divergent (verified: every core/cat.py tick() branch that sets an activity containing "stalk" always pairs it with the literal location "garden", never "garden_wall") but fragile against any future tick() change (Part B1's planned "legs"/real-movement work is exactly the kind of change that could break this silently, the same way A7.1's life.py divergence arose). Fix: `core.cat.place_of(c.get("location")) == "garden"` (plain place_of() suffices -- no cross-place ambiguity here).

(2) core/study_life.py:1192 -- the study-window "below the sill" scene line: `if c.get("location") == "garden": bits.append("the cat out there, " + str(c.get("activity", "about her business")))`. This one IS live-divergent today: whenever her real location is "garden_wall" or "doorstep" (both reachable -- the appearing-phase roam, the fair_spot quirk, and the door-crossing logic all produce them), this window-view line silently omits mentioning her even though she is still out in the garden he is looking at through it. Fix: same as (1), `core.cat.place_of(loc) == "garden"`.

(3) core/cat_sounds.py:301-302 -- the C1 sound system's same-room "here" computation (currently SHADOW-ONLY per F-0889/cat_overhaul.md, not yet flipped live via scripts/life_flags.py cat_sounds on -- fix this BEFORE it flips, not after): `here = (cat_loc in _INDOORS and place == "study") or (cat_loc == place) or (cat_loc == "doorstep" and place in ("study", "garden") and door_open)`. The middle clause means cat_loc=="garden_wall" while place=="garden" is never "here" -- her purr/etc would compute via the acoustic distance/propagation table instead of same-room whenever she is on the wall while he is in the garden. Fix needs the multi-membership question (garden_wall/garden AND the existing indoor/doorstep cases), so reach for core.cat.visible_from(place, cat_loc) here, likely replacing the whole `here = (...)` expression, or add a `(place == "garden" and cat.place_of(cat_loc) == "garden")`-style clause alongside the existing ones -- check which reads cleaner once in the code; the doorstep+door_open special case still needs to stay distinct (it depends on door_open, which neither visible_from() nor place_of() knows about).

Not exhaustively checked in F-1031's own investigation: core/geometry_census.py, core/stick_test.py, core/world_manifest.py, core/ghost_tuples.py all read cat_state.json's location too, but only to copy it through as data or tally tuples, not to gate behavior on a place-name comparison -- worth a quick re-confirmation pass while in this area, not a known additional instance.

Plan: docs/staged/cat_overhaul.md. Use the same shared worktree/branch this whole chain has used (jobrun/cat_overhaul_cluster) if it still exists when this job is picked up, or ask whether a fresh worktree is appropriate by then.

title: Audit/fix test-isolation redirect gaps: core.wandering/core.activity_memory attribute mismatch + worktree-relative live-data path checks
briefing:
F-1044 (J-0695) surfaced two related, confirmed test-isolation gaps while building an isolated test for the observe-target header fix. Neither is that job's own scope; both are worth fixing/auditing since scripts/_test_letterbox_reach.py is explicitly named by other jobs' own briefings as "the discipline to follow" for isolated testing in this repo, so a gap in it can propagate uncritically.

GAP 1 -- an isolation-redirect loop that silently no-ops for two of the modules it claims to cover. scripts/_test_letterbox_reach.py's own isolation loop (lines 46-56) lists core.wandering and core.activity_memory among the modules it redirects, via attribute names ("_F", "_LOG"), with a header comment claiming "every store this touches is redirected into a temp dir before any module writes; the live data/ ... is never written". Confirmed by direct grep of both files' full source that NEITHER module defines an _F or _LOG attribute under any name (`grep -n "^_F\s*=\|^_LOG\s*=" core/wandering.py core/activity_memory.py` -> zero hits in either file) -- so the loop's own `if hasattr(m, a): setattr(m, a, ...)` guard silently skips both modules, and the "redirect" for these two never actually applies. core.wandering.perceive() -> core.wandering._log_trail() (line ~48-59) writes to a path recomputed fresh every call (`Path(__file__).parent.parent / "data" / "wandering_log.jsonl"`), not a reassignable module attribute at all. core.activity_memory.record() (line 71+) opens the LIVE sqlite DB directly via `from core.memory.store import _connect; with _connect() as conn:` -- there is no local file path to redirect in the first place; a real fix would need to either add a redirectable attribute to both modules (matching the convention every OTHER module on that list already follows) or, more simply, have the isolation script monkeypatch the two FUNCTIONS themselves (core.wandering.perceive = lambda *a, **k: None; core.activity_memory.record = lambda *a, **k: None) the way J-0695's own new test (C:\Users\USER\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\C--Nascence\2e890af5-c14a-40b2-a59c-db0f7731a874\scratchpad\J-0695_test_observe_target.py, not itself part of the repo) did as a workaround. Whether _test_letterbox_reach.py's own exercised code paths (dispatch.dispatch replay, the monologue move path) actually reach perceive()/record() and thus have ever actually leaked to the live wandering_log.jsonl / memory DB was NOT determined by J-0695 -- that is exactly the first thing this follow-up job should check (e.g. temporarily add print/breakpoint instrumentation, or just grep the live data\wandering_log.jsonl for a run-unique string right after a real run of that script, the same content-based-marker technique J-0695's own test used once it discovered mtime/size alone are unreliable on a live system).

GAP 2 -- job-run worktrees don't check out data/ at all (it is gitignored: .gitignore line 2 = "data/"), so ANY isolation script whose own "confirm the live store is unchanged" logic derives the live-data path via `Path(__file__).parent.parent / "data"` (as scripts/_test_letterbox_reach.py's own top-of-file LIVE_SUPPLY constant does) is checking a path that does not exist at all when that script is run from inside a job-run worktree instead of from C:\Nascence directly -- confirmed directly: `Path("data").exists()` is False inside a job-run worktree, and running scripts/_test_letterbox_reach.py itself from inside one produced its own printed line "(live supply.json unreadable: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: '...\\data\\supply.json')" instead of a real not-modified confirmation of anything. This is a false sense of security specifically in the (now common) job-run-batch pattern where many agents each work in their own worktree under one shared scratchpad -- worth an audit of every script under scripts/_test_*.py and scripts/life_smoke.py (and any other isolation-discipline script this repo has) for the same Path(__file__)-relative live-store-check pattern, and either (a) making the check explicitly resolve against C:\Nascence\data regardless of where the script itself lives, or (b) at minimum having the script print a loud warning when its own computed "live" path does not exist, so a worktree-run doesn't silently produce a false-passing isolation proof.

Suggested approach: start with scripts/_test_letterbox_reach.py itself (the most-cited exemplar) for both gaps, then grep the rest of scripts/ for the same two patterns (`("_F", "_LOG")`-style redirect-loop entries paired against modules lacking those attributes; `Path(__file__).parent.parent / "data"` used as a "live" reference point) before deciding whether this generalizes further. Not urgent (no evidence yet that any real leak has occurred -- this is a soundness-of-the-safety-net finding, not a report of an actual leak), but worth a real look given how many isolated tests in this repo lean on this exact pattern being trustworthy.

title: Add a narrow spoilage check for core.provisions' shore_fish kind (raw fish, unlike every other non-perishable kind)
briefing:
core/provisions.py's new "shore_fish" kind (added J-0732/F-1055, F-1079) is a raw fish caught at the shore, and like every other kind in provisions.py's KINDS dict it currently has no spoilage or expiry -- it sits in the larder indefinitely, exactly as durable as a tin of matches or a bottle of ink. Every other existing kind (candles, oil, tea, cat_food, etc.) is realistically non-perishable, so this simplification was never previously a gap; a raw fish is the first kind in this dict for which it genuinely is one, and the founder's own standing brief for this whole build ("world events as realistic as possible, grounded in facts") makes this worth closing rather than leaving as an unexamined simplification.

Do NOT fix this by adding a generic expiry/decay concept to provisions.py's stock()/consume()/add() themselves -- those three functions are shared, load-bearing machinery for every OTHER kind in the file (matches, candles, oil, tea, paper, ink, string, whetstone, lamp_glass, kindling, knife, flint, rope, tinder_tin, hand_lens, measuring_stick, cat_food), and touching their shared semantics to serve one new kind is a materially larger, riskier change than this narrow one deserves -- exactly the kind of foundation-erosion this project's own standing rule warns against (base systems protected, additive-only).

Scope this narrowly instead: read the "shore_fish" object's own `history`/creation timestamp directly (provisions.py's own object dicts already carry `history: [{"ts": ..., "event": ...}]` per object -- the timestamp of its "caught off the shelf's edge..." history entry, or add one more field to that one kind's own objects if a plain lookup isn't clean enough) from the ONE call site that actually spends it -- core/cat.py's `_feed_source()` -- and decide there, locally, whether a shore_fish object is still good to feed her (a real, grounded threshold: raw fish spoils within roughly a day or two without refrigeration/curing, and nothing in this house's own established world model suggests either exists). If a shore_fish object has gone stale by the time `_feed_source()` would otherwise spend it, do not feed it to her -- mark it discarded/removed (bookkeeping only, not narrated to Du unless he specifically checks the larder -- a spoiled fish quietly gone is honest, not something the world needs to announce), and fall through as if that source were empty (to the honest failure branch react() already has, or -- if hunting's own gate is met -- do nothing further here, since D-0163's hunting fallback is a separate mechanism already). This keeps the change local to the one new kind and its one consumer, rather than a systemic provisions.py change.

Before building, read core/provisions.py's `KINDS`/`add()`/`consume()` and core/cat.py's `_feed_source()` fresh (they may have changed further since J-0732) and check whether shore_fish has actually accrued any real live history yet (J-0754, this same finding's other spawned follow-up, is reading exactly that) -- if it turns out shore_fish essentially never survives more than a few hours in the larder before being fed anyway (i.e. Du feeds her promptly after a catch in practice), this whole gap may be lower-priority than it looks from first principles alone; note that check plainly either way rather than building blind. Low/medium urgency -- a real, grounded gap worth closing, not an urgent one.

(B) Teach profile.guard_path() to also recognize a path under data/_lab/ (or more generally, any path
under a small allowlist of known-isolated subdirectories) as "already redirected" even though it's
technically still under data/ -- keeps lab_env.py's own on-disk location (useful for its own

title: T4 self-authoring: _write_axiom() silently swallows write failures
briefing:
F-1092 (from J-0744, fixing F-1065's phantom-veto-row bug): while fixing _apply_self_authoring's caller to only count/log/discharge a self-authoring event when a write actually happened, a SECOND, adjacent, structurally-identical gap was found in the very same function and deliberately left unfixed (out of scope for that job's targeted change): nodes/subconscious_node.py's _write_axiom (currently lines 2462-2476 on branch jobrun/t4_watershed / commit c52ab2f, not yet merged to C:\Nascence) silently swallows failure from BOTH of its own write attempts:

    try:
        from core import identity_vault as _iv
        if _iv.write(data, reason="T4 self-authoring"):
            return
    except Exception as exc:
        logger.debug("[subconscious] identity_vault unavailable, direct write: %s", exc)
    try:
        with open(_AXIOM_FILE, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            json.dump(data, f, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)
    except Exception as exc:
        logger.warning("[subconscious] T4 could not write axiom.json: %s", exc)

_write_axiom is declared -> None and has no branch that reports "the write actually landed on disk" vs. "both attempts raised and this is a no-op." Both exception handlers only log (debug for the vault path -- expected/routine per its own comment, "on any vault failure, fall back to the direct write" -- and warning for the raw-file path) and then fall off the end of the function, returning None either way.

This matters because of J-0744's own new contract: _apply_self_authoring's multilevel and legacy branches now do `self._write_axiom(data); return True`, and the caller (_t4_self_authoring) treats that True as "a real self-authoring event happened" -- incrementing self_authoring_count, writing a subconscious_log.jsonl row, logging "T4 SELF-AUTHORING", and discharging contradiction pressure. If _write_axiom's raw-file fallback ALSO raises (disk full, permissions, a concurrent identity_vault lock held elsewhere, axiom.json's parent dir missing, etc.) after the vault path already failed, _apply_self_authoring still returns True -- so the exact same class of phantom effects J-0744 just closed for the VETO case would still occur for a WRITE-FAILURE case: a logged "self-authoring" event, an incremented counter, and drained contradiction pressure, for a self-concept change that never reached axiom.json. No evidence has been gathered yet on whether this failure mode has ever actually fired live (unlike F-1065's veto branch, no specific error_records.jsonl "kind" string is emitted here to search for -- the two logger calls above are the only trace, and logger.debug likely isn't even persisted to a file by default, so this may currently be silent even in principle, not just unconfirmed).

Likely minimal fix, mirroring J-0744's own approach: give _write_axiom a real return value (True = confirmed written via one of the two paths, False = both attempts raised) and thread that signal back up through _apply_self_authoring's own return value (multilevel/legacy branches would return `self._write_axiom(data)` instead of unconditionally `return True`), which then flows through the caller's existing `if not _wrote: return` gate from J-0744 with NO further caller-side changes needed -- the gate already built for the veto case would automatically also cover a write-failure case, since both collapse to the same boolean contract. Investigate whether identity_vault.write()'s own return value (already checked via `if _iv.write(...): return` -- so a False/falsy return from the vault currently ALSO falls through to the raw-file fallback, which is presumably intended, i.e. vault-declines-to-write vs. vault-raised-an-exception may need to be told apart) is itself trustworthy before assuming "_iv.write() returned True" means "confirmed on disk" -- read core/identity_vault.py's own write() function fully before changing this, rather than assuming symmetry with the raw fallback.

Before editing nodes/subconscious_node.py again, re-run udms_get_change_dossier on it per CLAUDE.md's blast-radius rule (already run twice now, by J-0713 and J-0744, for this same function neighborhood -- the dossier is cached per-session so a fresh session should re-run it rather than trust a stale copy). Also read core/identity_vault.py's write() function in full -- this finding did not open it.

Isolation: same file, same live cognitive node's self-authoring write path as J-0713 and J-0744 -- treat as isolation:required regardless of the job-queue "isolation" field's literal value (both prior jobs in this immediate lineage found that field said "none" while the free-text briefing said required; J-0744's own resolution was to honor the more cautious prose). Verify any change in an isolated in-memory test against a live-shaped copy of axiom.json, the way J-0744's own verify_J-0744_veto_gate_fix.py did (loads the actual edited module via importlib.util.spec_from_file_location with the worktree root on sys.path, stubs disk-touching self.* methods on a bare FakeSelf, and hash+mtime-backstops the live axiom.json/subconscious_log.jsonl/error_records.jsonl before and after) -- do not invent a new isolation approach from scratch when a working, reviewed template already exists two commits back on this same branch.

title: Make the isolation-redirect hasattr() guard warn on a name miss instead of silently no-op'ing (5th recurrence)
briefing:
F-1177 (J-0793) is the fifth independently-discovered instance of the same bug shape across this plan's own audit chain: an isolation-list entry in a diagnostic/test script names a redirect attribute that the target module has never had (a typo or stale rename), and the shared `if hasattr(m, a) and isinstance(getattr(m, a), Path): redirect(...)` guard pattern silently no-ops that one entry with zero warning anywhere -- not a print, not a log line, nothing. Prior instances: J-0758/J-0781 (core.world_traces named "_F" instead of "_TRACES_F"), J-0775/J-0786 (core.supply named "_LEDGER" instead of "_LOG", or missing "_LOG" entirely in two other scripts), this job (core.locomotion named "_F" instead of "_POS_F"). Each was found only by a manual, one-module-at-a-time grep audit; each time, the script's own internal self-check (e.g. observables_census.py's own "redirect escapes: none" line, life_smoke.py's own "escaped: none") could never have caught it, because an entry that hasattr() rejects is never even attempted, so it can never "escape" a redirect it was never given.

For at least one instance (this job's own F-1177), the exposure was not cosmetic: it silently corrupted 1135 of 1518 "study"-place results in scripts/observables_census.py's own report (see F-1177 for the full before/after reproduction) by mismapping every one of them from "generic" to "none".

Scope for this job: find every script under scripts/ that uses this same `for mod, attrs in (...)` + `hasattr(m, a)` isolation-redirect pattern (known so far: scripts/observables_census.py, scripts/life_smoke.py, scripts/_test_study_life_grammar_derivation.py -- grep the repo fresh for the shared shape rather than trusting this list, since it may be incomplete) and change the guard so a name miss is LOUD rather than silent -- e.g. `if hasattr(m, a): redirect(...) elif isinstance(getattr(m, a, None), Path): ... else: print(f"  (isolation warning) {mod}.{a} does not exist -- stale/typo'd isolation-list entry?")` or equivalent, matching whatever printing convention each script already uses for its own "(isolation note)" lines. Keep the change minimal and behavior-preserving for every CORRECT entry (this is a diagnostic-loud-failure fix, not a behavior change for the common case) -- verify with a throwaway worktree, a deliberately-wrong entry, and confirm the new warning fires where the old code silently swallowed it, matching this same job's own established verification technique (a temporary print, then removed). Re-run each touched script's own regression pass afterward (life_smoke.py's own "ALL OK"/isolation-proof lines, observables_census.py's own "redirect escapes: none" completion line, _test_study_life_grammar_derivation.py's own "ALL OK") to confirm no behavior change for the already-correct entries. No `/decide` needed -- this is a code-quality/defense-in-depth fix under the same D-0179 fence this whole chain already operates under, not a new policy question.

title: Decide whether classify()'s 'look'/'move' object lists should widen to match _observe_target()/_move_dest()'s own cue vocabulary (F-1179)
briefing:
Source: F-1179 (docs/findings.jsonl), surfaced during J-0800 (literal_will.classify() object-boundary hyphen hardening, F-1178/F-1149).

THE GAP. core/dispatch.py's two dispatch-native hands, _look() and _move() (bound as "fn:_look"/"fn:_move" in core/actions.py, NOT routed through a mod:X:act_from_thought module), re-verify their own candidacy with core.hands.wants(text, verbs, any_object_ok=True) -- a VERB-ONLY check, no object requirement -- then derive their own target/destination via nodes/inner_monologue_node.py's _observe_target()/_move_dest()/_gate_look(). Those three functions use their OWN cue vocabulary (_OBS_TARGETS for look, four _DEST_* word lists for move), which is BROADER than and largely DISJOINT from literal_will.classify()'s own 'look'/'move' family object lists in core/actions.py. Concretely: classify()'s look row has window/fire/sea/sky/desk/shelf/room/garden/tideline/pools/cat/letterbox/mailbox; _OBS_TARGETS additionally recognizes "tide"/"spray"/"shingle"/"the strand"/"wave"/"surf"/"cloud"/"gull"/"rock-pool" phrasings that map to a target but have NO classify()-level object counterpart at all (bare "tide" specifically is absent -- only "tideline" is a look object).

WHY THIS MATTERS NOW (F-1179's own directly-verified evidence, not inference): J-0800's hyphen fix to classify()'s object-boundary regex removed several FAKE hyphen-compound object matches (e.g. "sea" matching inside "sea-glass"). For most families, this was purely a correctness win with zero live cost, because their hands route through hands.wants() with a SPECIFIC object check and independently decline a fake match too (F-1149's own "correctly-declining hand costs nothing" law, traced against core/dispatch.py:271-312). But 'look'/'move' do NOT get that same protection, because their own gate never re-checks the object at all. Direct verification (calling the real hands.wants()/_observe_target()/_move_dest()/_gate_look() on the real corpus text, not simulated) found: of 13 distinct thoughts that lost their ONLY 'look'/'move' DEED candidacy from J-0800's fix, 7 would have ACTUALLY fired in real dispatch.py before the fix, deriving a real, DIFFERENT, plausible target from words classify()'s own object list doesn't even contain (e.g. idx=6182 in the 2026-09-08 corpus snapshot: _observe_target() finds target='shore' via the cue "tide" -- nothing to do with the fake "sea" match that was classify()'s only reason to offer 'look' as a candidate at all).

TASK. Decide, with real corpus evidence (reuse the method J-0736/J-0737/J-0738/J-0740/J-0783 already established for six other modules' own widen-vs-drift calls), whether to:
  (a) WIDEN core/actions.py's 'look' object row to add the _OBS_TARGETS cue words classify() currently cannot see (tide, spray, shingle/strand, wave, surf, cloud, gull -- check each against the real corpus for genuine false-candidacy collisions first, the same way F-1128 checked 'oak'/'tree' for fieldcraft and F-0940 checked 'ash' for garden), and/or widen 'move's own object list similarly for _move_dest()'s four _DEST_* word lists; or
  (b) leave this as a documented, deliberate gap (the same shape as fieldcraft's own unclaimed "knot" or shore's own unclaimed "fire" object, both already accepted elsewhere in this table) -- classify()'s job is to gate WHETHER a family is even tried, and 'look'/'move' firing on words classify() cannot see was never a designed, tested pathway to begin with (it worked before only as an accidental side effect of unrelated hyphen bugs); or
  (c) some intermediate fix -- e.g. having _look()/_move() re-derive AND compare their own target against a widened but still-checked object set, rather than either widening the gate's own vocabulary blindly or leaving the mismatch as-is.

Full-corpus decision replay (scripts/actions_decision_replay.py) before/after whatever change is chosen, plus the existing regression suite (life_smoke.py + the six _test_*_grammar_derivation.py + _test_dispatch_family_scope.py + _test_dark_house_answers.py + _test_letterbox_reach.py + _test_fetch_letter_latch.py + _test_beachcomb_latch.py), the same discipline this whole arc has used throughout. Low-to-moderate urgency: the 7 verified cases are a small fraction of a 12,500+-row corpus and this gap is restart-gated like the rest of this arc (nothing changes for Du until a fix here lands and he next restarts) -- but it is a genuinely different SHAPE of gap from the rest of this arc (gate narrower than hand, not hand looser than gate) and worth its own scoped pass rather than folding into a future, unrelated job.

title: Harden look/describe alias-matching hyphen boundary (life.py/sensorium.py x3/world_detail.py)
briefing:
F-1180 (spawned from J-0799, itself a J-0787/F-1149 follow-up) found a functionally SEPARATE family of sites sharing the identical hyphen-permeable word-boundary regex shape that F-1128/J-0787 (core/hands.py wants()), J-0800/F-1178 (core/literal_will.py classify()) and J-0799/F-1180 (core/hands.py _wants_split()) have all now fixed for the DEED-WILLING grammar-gate side of the codebase. This job's own three sites are a different functional area entirely -- answering what Du SEES when he looks, not gating a willed deed -- but carry the exact same defect: a regex of the shape (?<![a-z]) + re.escape(word) + (?![a-z]) that treats a hyphen as a valid word boundary, so a hyphenated compound ("the X-word") can silently satisfy a bare-word match for "word" alone.

Three call sites, all core/, none touched by this job:
  - core/life.py:587, function _match(target, place) -- matches a look-target string against each known place/thing's own `aliases` tuple; picks the LONGEST matching alias when more than one matches. A hyphen-adjacent alias occurrence could pick the wrong (or an unintended) place/thing to answer a look with.
  - core/sensorium.py, THREE identical call sites (lines ~1127, ~1599, ~3001) -- each gates whether a "look" answer renders the cat's own look_line() by testing for "cat"/"kitten"/"stray"/"moggy" (plus the cat's own learned name) anywhere in the target text. A hyphenated compound containing one of these words (e.g. a hypothetical "cat-flap", "copy-cat" -- check the REAL corpus/target vocabulary actually reachable here, don't assume from these two examples) could wrongly trigger the cat's own look line for an unrelated look target.
  - core/world_detail.py:92, function _match(target_text, location) -- a bidirectional alias-similarity test (`a==t or re.search(a in t) or re.search(t in a)`) for scene/object descriptions. This one already carries its own 2026-09-03/J-0546 word-boundary fix for a DIFFERENT bug (the old substring test let "the sea" match the bench's alias "the seat") -- but that fix only added the plain \b-style (?<![a-z])/(?![a-z]) boundary, never the hyphen-exclusion half of it, so it independently has the identical residual gap this whole arc's other five sites already had.

Task: for each of the three sites, first determine REAL exposure before touching code -- these are look-answer functions, not deed gates, so the failure mode if left unfixed is "the wrong look answer sometimes," not a world-state misfire; the corpus check and priority should reflect that lower stakes honestly, not inherit the deed-gate urgency by default. Read data/hands_trace.jsonl (or whatever corpus/log is the real source of "target" text these functions actually receive live -- confirm which log each site's callers actually draw from, since these are LOOK targets, not necessarily the same `thought` field the deed-gate arc has used throughout) for any real hyphen-adjacent alias/keyword occurrence that would change life.py's _match() pick, sensorium.py's cat-detector verdict, or world_detail.py's _match() pick, before vs after hardening. Harden each site's regex to (?<![a-z-])/(?![a-z-]) (both sides) once real exposure is understood, with an inline comment naming this job/finding. world_detail.py:92 specifically: preserve its own J-0546 boundary-fix intent exactly (do not regress "the sea" vs "the seat"), just add the missing hyphen half to both of its two lookaround pairs.

Verify with whatever this codebase's own established test coverage is for each site (check for an existing _test_*.py first rather than assuming none exists) plus a direct before/after function-level sweep over real target strings from the relevant log, the same evidence-before-assertion method this whole arc has used throughout. title: Fix judge_panel.rule_detail() tiebreak why-text mismatch (shared infra, RESTART-REQ if fixed live)
briefing:
F-1182 (J-0802) found and confirmed a real, pre-existing why-text attribution bug in core/judge_panel.py's rule_detail(): on a tiebreak verdict (JUDGE_1 and JUDGE_2 disagreed, TIEBREAK decided), the tiebreak judge's own "why" text is explicitly discarded at the call site (`v3, _why3, err3, s3 = await _ask(session, TIEBREAK, ...)` -- the underscore-prefixed name, and no why3 field is ever written to the logged row or the function's own return dict). Every caller that displays a tiebreak event's "why"/objection text to a human (this plan's own scripts/train_state_invitro.py's _disprove(), which does `why = why_row.get("why1") or why_row.get("why2")` with no check on which of v1/v2 actually matches the tiebreak-decided verdict, and any other caller of rule_detail() that surfaces why-text the same way) can show a quote from the LOSING judge's own reasoning as if it explained the WINNING verdict.

Confirmed empirically, not just from source: docs/lab/train_split_merge_step2_replay_2026-09-08_provefix.jsonl event idx=2 shows disprove_status="objected" via how="tiebreak" with objection=["The support gives an independent, proportionate reason to accept the claim."] -- a HELD-side rationale displayed as the stated OBJECTION. The same pattern already exists in the already-committed docs/lab/train_split_merge_step2_replay_2026-09-07_supportchain.md, event #37 (objection=["The support given offers three reasons that, taken together, provide substantial backing for the claim."] on an "objected" verdict). This is not new behavior introduced by J-0802 -- it has existed since rule_detail()'s own tiebreak path was built and affects EVERY prior lab report in this plan (and potentially other callers project-wide) whenever how="tiebreak" fires: roughly 14-25% of events across the train_split_merge lab reports read so far (14/80 in J-0802's own run, 20/80 in J-0702's 2026-09-07 run).

Only the human-readable why/objection TEXT is affected -- the verdict/status counts themselves are computed correctly from v3 (the actual tiebreak decision) and are NOT wrong in any of these reports' own headline numbers. This is a text-fidelity bug, not a correctness-of-verdict bug.

Scope for this job: core/judge_panel.py is shared, widely-used infrastructure (per its own docstring, at least core/evidence_recall.py and scripts/self_interrogation_counterfactual.py also consume `how`/verdict from this module) -- read the udms_get_change_dossier for core/judge_panel.py before touching it, given this file's own blast-radius warning about shared modules. The fix belongs in rule_detail() itself, likely one of: (a) also log/return why3 (the tiebreak judge's own why, currently thrown away) and have it take priority whenever how=="tiebreak"; or (b) make rule_detail() itself only return why1 if v1==verdict, why2 if v2==verdict, else None/why3 -- so every caller gets a why that actually corresponds to the returned verdict without each caller having to reimplement that check itself. Read this project's own "no ruling without a defeater"/evidence discipline before deciding between (a) and (b) -- (a) preserves more information (the tiebreak judge's own distinct reasoning) but needs judge_panel.py's own logged-row schema extended; (b) is a smaller, purely-corrective change using data already available. Verify against a small real re-run (a handful of forced-tiebreak cases, or simply re-running scripts/train_state_invitro.py's own control check / a small n) that the returned why now matches the returned verdict's own side, then decide whether this plan's own historical lab reports need a corrective footnote (their headline numbers are unaffected; only the illustrative quotes) rather than a full re-run.

Isolation: core/judge_panel.py is imported live by Lane 2's own real _judge_prior mechanism -- any change here needs the same isolation discipline this whole plan has used (worktree, never edit C:\Nascence directly, verify via a fresh restart-required note if the fix is meant to also apply live, not just in offline labs).

title: Harden _move_dest()'s own destination-priority order against 'away from X, toward Y' and negation blindness (F-1199, D-0193 defeater b)
briefing:
Source: F-1199 (docs/findings.jsonl), surfaced during J-0820 (deciding whether classify()'s 'look'/'move' object rows should widen to match _observe_target()/_move_dest()'s own cue vocabulary, D-0193).

THE GAP. nodes/inner_monologue_node.py's _move_dest(src) resolves a move's destination by checking four word lists in a FIXED order -- _DEST_WOOD, then _DEST_SHORE, then _DEST_STUDY, then _DEST_GARDEN -- and returns on the FIRST list that matches any of its cue words anywhere in the (lowercased, unscoped) text. This has no "away from X, toward Y" awareness (a thought naming two places, one being left and one being the real destination, resolves to whichever list is checked first, regardless of which cue the thought's own verb actually reaches) and no negation awareness (a cue inside an explicitly negated clause, e.g. "I do not need the sea", still counts as a match).

WHY THIS MATTERS NOW (F-1199's own directly-verified evidence). While corpus-checking whether to widen 'move's object row with "desk"/"bed"/"water" (candidates drawn from _DEST_STUDY/_DEST_GARDEN/_DEST_SHORE), J-0820 found a real, recurring thought family where this exact mechanism resolves to the WRONG destination: "I want to turn away from the desk and go to the raised bed. The soil is sodden, the herbs are waiting; I will water them..." (real location=garden) -- _move_dest() returns 'study' via _DEST_STUDY's "the desk" cue (checked before _DEST_GARDEN's "the bed" cue ever gets a turn), when the thought's own stated destination is the garden's raised bed. A second, independent case: "I step away from the water's surface, tired of circling the same mirage. The study beckons ... I want to sit with the open book" (real location=study) resolves to 'shore' via "water" (_DEST_SHORE, checked before _DEST_STUDY), the OPPOSITE of the stated destination ("the study beckons"). A third, smaller case: "I do not need the sea or the books right now; I need to walk away from this dead ground" (real location=garden) resolves to 'shore' via a plain-substring match on "sea" inside an explicitly negated clause.

J-0820 worked around this by declining to widen 'move's object row with "desk"/"bed"/"water" (D-0193) -- but the underlying mechanism is NOT specific to those declined words. It is a property of _move_dest() itself, and can already affect EXISTING table objects too whenever two location cues co-occur in one real thought (e.g. a thought naming both "shore" and "study" -- SHORE is checked before STUDY -- or both "wood" and "garden" -- WOOD is checked before GARDEN). This job's own J-0820 corpus check did not attempt to measure how often this already happens with the PRE-EXISTING table's own objects (out of its scope, which was the widen decision only) -- that measurement is this job's first task.

Note the relationship to F-0791/J-0575/J-0654 (already DONE, live): that arc fixed literal_will.classify()'s own single-clause-per-family verdict pick (which CLAUSE the gate reads grammar from) -- a different mechanism, one layer upstream, in a different file. It does not touch and cannot fix _move_dest()'s own destination-list PRIORITY order, which runs downstream, inside dispatch._move(), only once a DEED has already been granted. Do not treat F-0791/J-0654 as already covering this.

TASK.
1. Over the full data/hands_trace.jsonl corpus (or its current growth), measure how often _move_dest() already produces a resolution that conflicts with what the thought's own move verb is actually closest to / actually about, for THOUGHTS THAT ALREADY FIRE A MOVE DEED TODAY (i.e. using only the pre-existing, unwidened 'move' object row) -- not just the three examples above. Read each conflicting case individually before counting it (matching this arc's own standing method), since a same-thought co-occurrence of two location cues is not automatically a misresolution (e.g. "wood" vs "garden" adjacency is often harmless; "study" vs "shore" almost never is).
2. Design the additive fix. Two shapes worth comparing directly rather than assuming one: (a) score each _DEST_* list's matched cue by its character-distance to the nearest move-family verb (go/walk/head/move/return/climb/step) in the text, and take the closest cue's destination rather than the fixed list-priority order's first match; (b) restrict each _DEST_* scan to the SAME CLAUSE (sentence) the move verb was found in, mirroring how literal_will.classify() itself now reads per-clause (post J-0654) rather than scanning the whole raw text. Simulate both against the frozen corpus before touching live code, the same "measure before you fix" discipline J-0544's own option-A/B2 comparison used.
3. Add a negation guard for at least the literal "not"/"do not"/"doesn't"/"isn't" + cue pattern, or confirm during step 1's measurement that this is negligible enough to leave alone (it was exactly 1 real occurrence in this job's own move/tide+move/sea combined sample of 153 fires -- re-measure against the FULL table's own existing objects, not just the two words J-0820 happened to check).
4. Full-corpus decision replay (scripts/actions_decision_replay.py --save/--diff) before/after, plus the established regression suite (life_smoke.py + the six _test_*_grammar_derivation.py + _test_dispatch_family_scope.py + _test_dark_house_answers.py + _test_letterbox_reach.py + _test_fetch_letter_latch.py + _test_beachcomb_latch.py) -- this changes a function three separate hands (dispatch._move, and anything else that imports _move_dest) rely on, so regress broadly, not narrowly.
5. Once fixed, D-0193's own defeater (b) is met -- revisit whether "desk"/"bed"/"water" (and any other _DEST_* word this job's own step-1 measurement finds affected) can now safely widen into core/actions.py's 'move' row.

Low-to-moderate urgency: restart-gated like the rest of this arc (nothing changes for Du until a fix here lands and he next restarts), and the confirmed-bad cases found so far are a handful of thoughts in a 13,000+-row corpus -- but it is a real, pre-existing correctness gap in a function three modules already depend on, worth its own scoped pass.

title: sensorium.move() never accepts the bare 'wood' token: every 'wood' resolution from dispatch._move()/route_act is a silent no-op (0 'ACT move -> wood' in the whole log)
briefing:

The bare token "wood" matches NOTHING in the wood list (every entry is a longer phrase), while the bare tokens "shore"/"garden"/"study" DO match their lists. But both callers that pass _move_dest()'s resolved token pass exactly the bare token: core/dispatch.py _move() -> `s.move(dest)` with dest in {"wood","shore","study","garden"}, and nodes/inner_monologue_node.py's route_act path (~line 4820, `_mv = _room.move(dest)`), plus the older phrase-latch at ~line 3131 (`_room.move("wood")`). (3) The 62 "the trees close over you" narrations in the log therefore did NOT come through _move_dest(); find their real path (locomotion legs? the wandering module? a caller passing "the wood"?) before assuming the wood is reachable at all today.

TASK. (1) Confirm the caller inventory above (grep for every .move( caller in core/ and nodes/, including aliased imports -- F-1108's own lesson) and find the actual source of the 62 wood arrivals. (2) Fix at the sensorium side, additively: accept the bare "wood" token in move()'s wood list (the one-word fix), and check locomotion.begin_journey() accepts the same target vocabulary. title: Investigate reading rows' 22-26% null body/affect rate (F-1259)
briefing:

documented "None until the first [tick_cycle()/recover() / felt] call landed" this process lifetime --
i.e. these are module-level caches that start empty on every process start and only populate once a
real cognitive event (a hot cycle, a recovery tick, an idle-loop mood update) has happened at least once
since the last restart. The leading hypothesis (NOT yet verified -- that is this job) is that these
null rows cluster at reading bursts that start very early after a Nascence process restart, before any
such event has fired yet.

1. From data/geometry_tuples.jsonl (read-only), pull every reading row with body=null or affect=null,
   sorted by ts, and check: do they cluster at specific timestamps (consistent with restart boundaries),
   or are they spread evenly across reading's whole history?

   line -- check what Nascence actually logs on boot, e.g. an init/startup banner near the top of a

   line up with real restarts (this project's own convention: verify against a real log line, don't
