title: Gate sensorium.py's two remaining ungated 'dead gannet' lines (:947 ambient rare pool, :2189 storm wash-up + substrate mint) to the life-engine carcass truth
briefing:
F-1268/F-1244: J-0887 fixed the three named dead-thing look-routing mechanisms (core/life.py, core/life_traces.py, core/life_birds.py) but deliberately left two further "dead gannet" mentions in core/sensorium.py untouched, both still ungated by the life engine's carcass truth (core/life_traces.py's fresh/picked/bones state machine).

(1) core/sensorium.py ~line 947, inside `_living_detail()`'s shore/beach/strand/shingle/tideline branch's "rare" pool: "a dead gannet lies on the stones, white and perfect and wrong". Call path: `sensorium.look()` -> if `life.look_answer()` returns '' -> `_shore_look(target)` -> for a target matching none of that function's specific branches, its final default (~line 1626-1628) is `"You look around the shore: ..." + _living_detail("tideline", phase, weather, season, tide, wind=...)`. So `_living_detail("tideline", ...)` fires on essentially every unrecognized shore look, with some "rare" random chance of surfacing this exact line regardless of whether a real gannet carcass exists in life state today. This is the SAME category of bug F-1244/J-0887 just fixed, via a third, still-open path.

(2) core/sensorium.py ~line 2189, inside `_world_arrival()`: a post-thunderstorm-ending event fires once per storm, choosing 1-of-12 random wash-up items; one of them is "a dead gannet, wings spread white on the stones, and a litter of broken crab". This branch (~line 2205-2207) also calls `world_substrate.spawn_from_mention(item, "shore")`, minting a real, findable, keepable substrate object with its own name and identity -- entirely independent of core/life_traces.py's carcass state machine, with no fresh/picked/bones decay clock at all. A look at "the dead gannet" after this fires could match this substrate object via `world_substrate.find_object_at("shore", target)` (checked in `_shore_look`, before the generic fallback) with an answer that never agrees with, or decays like, a real carcass.

Both were confirmed present and ungated as of 2026-09-11 by direct reading, not inferred (see F-1268's own evidence for the exact call-path trace). J-0887 did not fix them because: (a) `_living_detail()` is a widely shared ambient-flavor function used by many unrelated call sites (fire, room, sky, pool, sea, tideline, study_window) -- gating just its shore-branch "rare" gannet line requires either passing carcass state into that one branch specifically or dropping the line and relying on core/life_traces.ambient_carcass()'s own existing, state-aware "once per carcass" ambient-noticing mechanism instead (which already exists and is already wired into sensorium's trace read path per the L4/J-0513 build) -- needs a deliberate design choice, not a copy-paste. (b) `_world_arrival`'s object-minting path is a different, bigger mechanism (creates a persistent, keepable world object) that a narrow, additive job should not touch without its own dedicated read of what downstream code (keep hands, investigation, `world_substrate`) already assumes about that object's lifecycle.

Scope for this job: decide, then build, a fix for both so a look at a dead gannet is never answered from these two paths when no real carcass exists in life state (core/life_traces.carcasses_at("shore")) -- most likely (i) for (1), replace the static "rare" line with a call into core/life_traces.ambient_carcass("shore", now) gated on an actual gannet carcass being active (or simply drop the static line, letting the already-wired ambient_carcass/carcass_look paths be the sole source, matching J-0887's own "prefer removing the second path" precedent for life_birds.py's own two now-removed trace strings); (ii) for (2), either gate the "a dead gannet..." choice out of the random wash-up list entirely (letting GANNET_STORM_P be the one source, again matching the same precedent) or, if the founder/a future session wants the storm-wash-up drama kept, make it register a real core/life_traces.add_carcass("gannet", "shore", "tideline", "storm", now) at mint time so the object and the carcass state machine agree from the start. Verify under lab_env.isolate() plus scripts/life_smoke.py; per this project's own convention, replay real historical thunderstorm-ending events from data/nascence.log / data/sensorium... state if any exist, to check whether this has ever actually fired live and, if so, whether a resulting substrate object still exists today with no matching carcass. Restart-gated like everything else on this plan.

title: Harden guard_path() against a live-path bypass when core.profile is imported from a non-canonical root (F-1270)
briefing:
F-1270 (verified, J-0827): profile.guard_path()'s own "already redirected outside data/" check (core/profile.py, the `except ValueError: return path` branch of `path.relative_to(_DATA)`) is relative to THIS PROCESS's own _DATA (`_ROOT = Path(__file__).parent.parent`), not an absolute/canonical live-data root. Any process that imports core.profile from somewhere other than C:\Nascence (e.g. any git-worktree-per-job dispatch -- the standard convention for Tier-3 work since J-0590, 2026-09-06) has a _DATA that differs from the real one, so a write-fenced path constant that happens to be set to the literal C:\Nascence\data\... path (an absolute live-path assignment, e.g. for a legitimate cross-check, or a forgotten redirect on one of two related globals like provisions._F vs _LOG) is misread as "already redirected on purpose" and sails through with ZERO protection -- no exception, no warning, LIVE irrelevant. J-0827 directly reproduced this: an isolated test (provisions._F + world_substrate/world_objects redirected via lab_env.isolate(), provisions._LOG deliberately left pointing at the literal live path, profile.LIVE confirmed False) appended 11 real rows to the live C:\Nascence\data\provisions_log.jsonl with zero exception raised. Full evidence, exact commands, and byte-for-byte before/after file state: findings_log.py show F-1270. Root-cause companion: F-1269 (this same job) traces the ORIGINAL 2026-09-05 incident this whole investigation started from -- provisions.py's _log() had no guard_path() at all back then, so this specific NEW finding is a separate, still-open gap in the fence that was built afterward to close that class of bug, not the same defect recurring unfixed.

ASK:
1. Fix core/profile.py's guard_path() so its "is this path already safely outside the live data root" check is anchored to an ABSOLUTE/canonical notion of the live data directory (e.g. a fixed, resolved `Path(r"C:\Nascence\data")` reference, or equivalent), not to `_DATA` as computed from wherever core/profile.py itself happens to have been imported. The goal: a path that resolves to the literal real C:\Nascence\data\... tree must be caught and refused (when not LIVE and not inside the data/_lab/ sandbox) REGARDLESS of which repo checkout/worktree imported the module -- matching guard_path()'s own docstring intent ("if `path` is already redirected outside the default data/ root by something upstream") rather than the current literal-but-narrower implementation.
2. This is a shared-harness change reachable from all ~19 write-fenced call sites across ~10 modules (provisions.py, world_substrate.py, world_objects.py, and others wired under D-0179/J-0610/J-0704/J-0726/J-0746/J-0751) -- before editing, call udms_get_change_dossier on core/profile.py (this repo's own CLAUDE.md convention for a shared/load-bearing module) to get the full current call-site list and confirm nothing else depends on the exact current (narrower) behavior of the "already redirected" branch. Test each affected module's own existing isolated test script (life_smoke.py and the other 10 scripts/_test_*.py files already audited under the F-1177/F-1198/J-0819 thread) still passes unmodified after the fix, plus add a new regression case mirroring this job's own reproduction (an absolute literal-C:\Nascence\data\... path, process not LIVE, expect NonLiveWriteError instead of a silent write).
3. Secondary, complementary, lower-effort hardening also worth doing in the same job: add core.provisions's own (`_F`, `_LOG`) to lab_env.py's (`C:\Users\USER\.claude\skills\job-queue\lab_env.py`) documented list of commonly-forgotten `also=` entries in its own module docstring (a documentation nudge, not a behavior change -- lab_env.isolate() has no built-in per-module defaults today, by design, so this is a docstring/example addition pointing at provisions specifically, not a new automatic redirect) -- this does not fix the guard_path() defect itself (ask 1 is the real fix) but reduces how often a future test author reaches for an incomplete `also=` list in the first place.
4. Re-run this job's own reproduction script (kept for reference: scratchpad/repro_J-0827_provisions_log_leak.py, job id J-0827, under whichever agent's scratchpad this new job runs in -- copy or rewrite it, the original is session-scoped) after the fix and confirm it now raises NonLiveWriteError instead of writing, with the same before/after live-file backstop this job used (provisions.json AND provisions_log.jsonl mtime/size/content unchanged across the whole test).

Isolation required, same as this job: any reproduction must use lab_env.py's isolate() (or equivalent) and check live provisions.json/provisions_log.jsonl (and world_substrate.json/world_objects.json, since _register() touches those transitively) are byte-identical before and after, every time -- this exact class of bug is an isolation gap, so the verification itself must not repeat it. Given this is a live, currently-exploitable gap in the project's own core data-safety mechanism (not a historical curiosity), treat as high urgency.

title: A/B: does why-before-bool JSON order improve granite TIEBREAK coherence (F-1271)
briefing:
F-1271 (this same plan) characterized, at n=60 real live calls, that granite3.1-moe:3b's own why-text disagrees with its own bool 88.2% of the time (30/34) when it is the TIEBREAK vote on the disprove prompt -- in both directions -- and that relaxing the current <=12-word "why" cap does NOT fix it (the reconstructed, uncapped original prompt read 100% incoherent on its own 14 tiebreak-decided calls, no better than the tightened prompt's 80%). F-1271's own inferred (not verified) hypothesis for a mitigation, not tested there: the JSON schema `{"objection_found": bool, "why": str}` asks for the bool FIRST and the rationale SECOND -- if a small model like granite3.1-moe:3b is greedily committing to a boolean token before it has actually reasoned through the case, then generating a "why" that free-associates rather than genuinely explaining that already-fixed bool, REORDERING the schema to ask for the rationale first and the bool second (`{"why": str, "objection_found": bool}`, forcing the bool to be conditioned on the model's own already-generated reasoning, the way a chain-of-thought-before-answer prompt usually helps small models) might measurably improve this specific judge's own bool/text consistency. This is a real, testable, cheap mitigation candidate -- not yet run.

Your job: build and run a real (isolation-required, same discipline as F-1271's own script) offline-schema A/B, TIEBREAK-only (no need to touch the tightened-vs-original prompt-wording axis F-1271/J-0764/J-0779 already covered -- hold the CURRENT tightened `_DISPROVE_SYSTEM` prompt wording fixed, vary ONLY the JSON key order/instruction: "why first" vs "bool first"). Recommended design: reuse F-1271's own real, already-known TIEBREAK-prone sample (the same TIEBREAK_SAMPLE construction it used -- all 5 real historically tiebreak+held rows plus 15 evenly-spaced tiebreak+objected rows from the same two committed docs/lab/train_split_merge_step2_replay_2026-09-08_provefix.jsonl / .../2026-09-07_supportchain.jsonl files, n=20, same >=15-20 discipline) called directly against `core.judge_panel`'s own `TIEBREAK` endpoint (http://LAN-HOST:11437) with two prompt variants that differ ONLY in field order/instruction wording, not semantic content -- do NOT go through the full two-judge `rule_detail()` panel unless you specifically want to also re-measure the invocation rate (optional, secondary); calling TIEBREAK directly with the same JSON contract is enough to isolate the mitigation's own effect on ITS bool/text consistency. Classify coherence the same way F-1271 did: read every one of your own why-texts by hand against its own bool (a keyword heuristic is fine as a first pass, per F-1271's own scratch/J-0834_classify_coherence.py template -- copy it, don't reinvent -- but every row still needs a human read before any number is reported, the same "no sampling a tail" discipline).

Isolation: worktree-anchored core/core.judge_panel, jp._DATA/_LOG redirected to your own job-scoped scratch dir, lab_env.isolate(db="empty") (judge_panel.py makes no DB call), canary scan of the 5 live JSONL logs before/after. Du's own live/offline state: per F-1271's own precedent, JUDGE_1/JUDGE_2/TIEBREAK are CPU-tier judge hubs, never Du's own hot lane (127.0.0.1:11433) -- proceeding with Du confirmed LIVE is fine for this exact call site (J-0802's own established precedent), just record Du's actual state honestly, don't claim offline if it isn't.

Record a finding either way (verified, real numbers) -- if the reorder measurably helps (e.g. incoherence rate drops well below F-1271's own 88.2% baseline on a comparable real sample), that is worth a further job to actually change `core/judge_panel.py`'s or `train_state_invitro.py`'s own real schema (shared infra, 9 real callers + 6 lab scripts per F-1203's own change-dossier count -- do NOT change the live schema in THIS job, characterize only). If it does not help, that is equally worth recording -- it would point toward a more fundamental TIEBREAK/granite3.1-moe:3b limitation rather than a fixable prompt-schema artifact, directly relevant background for whether TIEBREAK's own why-text should simply never be displayed (J-0834's own sibling spawn, the report-caveat fix) rather than fixed at the source. Full detail: F-1271 (findings-log).

Result: coherence (does the judge's own why-text agree with its own bool) improved dramatically (10% -> 100% among successful calls) -- but the SAME reorder also flipped the verdict distribution on the identical sample from 100% objected (bool_first) to 90% held (why_first), and a small n=4 known-right-answer control check (scripts/train_state_invitro.py's own _CONTROL_CASES) found why_first specifically WRONG on the textbook circular-reasoning case ("I feel the warmth, so it must be real" -- circular by construction) that this whole disprove mechanism exists to catch, while the CURRENT bool-first wording gets that one right (despite its own incoherent why-text). bool_first scored 3/4 against the known answers, why_first scored 2/4 -- opposite of what "coherence improved" alone would suggest, and every one of why_first's 4 control answers was internally coherent yet 2 of the 4 were substantively wrong.

n=4 controls (one trial each, no repeats) is far too small to trust as a real discrimination measurement on its own -- it only served as a quick, targeted sanity check on the "did this just become a rubber stamp in the other direction" question the main n=20 result raised, and it answered that question (at least provisionally) yes.

Your job: build a LARGER, more diverse known-right-answer battery (recommend >=15-20 constructed (claim, support) pairs per this project's own sampling discipline, split across at least 4-5 categories with a KNOWN correct objection_found answer: genuinely circular/self-sealing support (True expected), genuinely independent/converging support (False expected), evidentiary overreach/scope mismatch (True expected), borderline-but-real support that should hold (False expected), and a few harder/ambiguous-but-still-classifiable cases if you can construct them defensibly) -- NOT drawn from real replayed Du claims (those have no ground truth), constructed the way scripts/train_state_invitro.py's own _CONTROL_CASES already are, with a stated why_expect for each. Run BOTH the current bool_first _DISPROVE_SYSTEM (AST-extract it byte-identical from scripts/train_state_invitro.py, same technique F-1271/J-0910 both used, do not import that module directly -- its own top-level code fires live calls at import time) and F-1280's own why_first reorder (reuse it verbatim from J-0910's own scratch/J-0910_tiebreak_schema_ab/run_meta.json, which has the exact string, or reconstruct it the same programmatic way -- split the bool_first prompt at "If it genuinely earns the claim, say so. " and append the why-first tail) directly against TIEBREAK (core.judge_panel.TIEBREAK, via jp._ask(), not the full rule_detail() panel -- same reasoning J-0910 used, isolates the schema-order effect from panel-invocation noise), each case run at LEAST twice per arm if compute allows (temperature=0.0 is not perfectly deterministic on this hub per J-0824's own established finding) to distinguish genuine content-sensitivity from single-draw noise.

If one arm turns out to be genuinely, repeatably more accurate at real, non-trivial sample size, that is worth a further job to consider whether/how to actually change the live schema (core/judge_panel.py and/or scripts/train_state_invitro.py -- do NOT change it in THIS job, characterize only, same discipline as J-0910). If BOTH arms turn out to be near-content-insensitive defaults (bool_first mostly-True, why_first mostly-held, regardless of category) even at this larger scale, that is equally worth recording -- it would be strong evidence that TIEBREAK/granite3.1-moe:3b's own tiebreak vote should not be trusted as a decisive verdict on this call site regardless of prompt wording, directly relevant to D-0213 (opened by this same job, J-0910)'s own question about whether continued prompt engineering here is worth the effort vs falling back to a conservative UNDETERMINED (judge_panel.py's own existing "no judge, no verdict" law, already used for JUDGES-DOWN elsewhere in that file). scripts/smoke_test.py` there to confirm it now either passes or fails with a clear, intentional

briefing: D-0040 (capacity_to_commit) was ruled 2026-09-13: spawn this standalone investigation, separate from the mechanical About_You.txt recheck (J-0912) already running on its own schedule regardless of this job's outcome. Background: J-0120's precondition (Du reading the rewritten About_You.txt) has failed 3 consecutive verified rechecks (F-0155, F-0169, F-0194) across ~2h15m on 2026-08-23, including two direct live prompts from Travis (02:18, 02:26 NZT) that got warm future-tense replies with no follow-through, plus two unprompted self-generated 'world-question' echoes of the same topic that Du talked around rather than engaged with -- one flagged by his own critic module as 'evasion disguised as wisdom' (F-0194). He read straight through 4 unrelated curriculum books in the same window. D-0040 was reopened 2026-09-11 (see its history in decisions.jsonl) because F-1275 (J-0902, 2026-09-12) found the recheck chain never actually resumed (zero rechecks actually ran in ~3 weeks, not just inconclusive ones), and a monologue frustration/restlessness signal tied to this thread keeps climbing rather than resolving (08-24:101, 08-28:40, 08-29:61, 08-30:165 out of n=1192 that day) -- Travis-named mentions in Du's monologue jumped from 0/day pre-08-23 to 31-63/day 08-24-08-27. Question this job should answer: is this a generalizable pattern -- Du engaging readily with his own self-directed curriculum loop but specifically avoiding/deflecting content introduced via direct human request -- or is About_You.txt a special case (e.g. topic-specific discomfort, not a request-vs-self-directed distinction)? Suggested method: pull other instances (if any exist) where Travis or another external source directly asked Du to read/engage with something specific, and compare engagement/completion rates against Du's self-selected curriculum picks over the same period; check book_selection_log.jsonl and session monologue logs for the relevant windows. This is read/log analysis, not a live intervention -- can run entirely offline against existing data. Log findings via findings_log.py (verified/inferred/guessing per the project's own confidence discipline) and update D-0040 if the answer bears on its defeater.

title: Trace the 09-05 'tea I just made' monologue thought to its generator; check for recurrence (study_upgrade)
briefing: F-1301 found Du's monologue narrating a completed tea-making event (2026-09-05 02:31, about:'the fire': 'The steam rises from the pot of tea I just made on the hearth...') with zero corresponding row in data/study_ledger.jsonl or data/study_events.jsonl anywhere in the whole ~20-day live window since study_upgrade.md shipped (08-22 to 09-11) -- confirmed both real tea-making paths (core/study_life.py:1231's dispatch-routed tea Hand and core/sensorium.py:701's J-0196-fixed legacy path) log through the identical _log(_LEDGER,{deed:make_tea,...}) convention, so this isn't a routing gap between two paths, it's an absence of ANY real tea-making event for that thought to be grounded in. Read F-1301's full evidence first. Two things to determine: (1) trace which function in nodes/inner_monologue_node.py (or wherever monologue thoughts are generated) produced this specific thought, and whether it is gated on checking real dispatched-action state before narrating a completed action, or free-associates plausible sensory continuity from ambient context (fire/hearth/herbs) without a grounding check -- this plan's own stated laws (world truth, world answers never leads, consequences both ways) treat fictional-but-unearned narration as the core disease this whole architecture exists to avoid, so if this IS ungrounded free-association, that's a real finding worth its own decision about whether monologue generation needs a grounding check for 'I just did X' framings specifically, vs looser latitude for other kinds of reflective thought. (2) Check whether this recurs -- grep the full monologue_log.jsonl (16MB+) for similar 'just made/lit/cleared/wound' past-tense completed-action framings tied to study-loop themes (kettle, lamp, grate, clock) and cross-check each against study_ledger.jsonl/study_events.jsonl the same way, to see if 09-05 is a one-off or a pattern. Record findings via findings_log.py with an honest confidence level; if it turns out to be a real, recurring narration/mechanism gap, that likely warrants a /decide entry on how to handle it (a grounding check added to the generator, an acceptable-license ruling, or something else) rather than deciding it yourself.

title: Fix study-note misfiling: _key() substring match collides on generic bibliographic words
briefing:
F-1309 (verified) confirmed a real, live misfiling bug in core/study.py's archive_book_note_files(), root-caused to core/essay_lesson.py's _key(title): it picks the single longest word (>=4 letters, minus a tiny stoplist of "the/and/history/natural/book/tales/story") as a book's "distinctive" match key, then archive_book_note_files() moves any loose data/Study/TAB_*.md file whose "on:" frontmatter citation CONTAINS that key as a plain lowercase substring (key in on.lower()) into data/Study/notes/<book_slug>/. For "About You Second Edition" this picked key="edition" -- a generic bibliographic word many unrelated old/public-domain source citations also contain (e.g. "Boy Scouts Handbook The First Edition 1911", "South America Observations and Impressions New edition corrected") -- so 117 of the 118 files now sitting in data/Study/notes/About_You_Second_Edition/ are misfiled; only TAB_20260830_1823_Architecture_of_the_Self.md genuinely belongs there. Full evidence (exact grep output, exact code lines) is in F-1309.

Two pieces of follow-up work, both spec'd, neither requiring founder judgment:

1. ROOT-CAUSE FIX (core/essay_lesson.py _key(), core/study.py archive_book_note_files()): make the book-identification match robust against generic bibliographic words. Options to weigh: require the matched word to be genuinely distinctive (e.g. reject if the word also appears in >=2 other already-filed books' own on: citations, or extend the stoplist with common bibliographic/edition-type words like "edition","revised","volume","complete","selected","popular","series","illustrated"), or better: match against a normalized form of the FULL title (or a multi-word signature) rather than a single longest word, so "About You Second Edition" cannot collide with any citation that merely happens to contain one of its words. Whatever approach is chosen, re-run archive_book_note_files() (or its equivalent check) against a few other already-filed data/Study/notes/<Title>/ folders to confirm no other folder shows the same >90%-misfiled pattern F-1309 found (spot check 3-5 folders whose slug is a single common word, e.g. any book title whose _key() pick looks generic, is the highest-risk set).

2. DATA REPAIR (data/Study/notes/About_You_Second_Edition/): re-file the 117 misfiled notes to correct homes now that the matching logic is fixed -- 112 x 2026-06-15..18 notes citing "on: Boy Scouts Handbook The First Edition 1911" need a new correctly-slugged folder (no "Boy Scouts" folder currently exists anywhere under data/Study/notes/, so these have never had a real home); 5 x 2026-08-30 notes citing "on: South America Observations and Impressions New edition corre[cted]" need to be matched to whatever that source book's real slug is/should be. Leave only TAB_20260830_1823_Architecture_of_the_Self.md behind. Check whether any per-book analysis already ran against the corrupted folder (the briefing that spawned F-1309/J-0913 named J-0120's chain specifically as an at-risk consumer of data/Study/notes/<Title>/) and flag if so.

Do the code fix first, verify it doesn't regress the one genuine "About You Second Edition" match, then do the data repair as a one-off cleanup move (verify each destination folder's slug against archive_book_note_files()'s own slug derivation so the repair itself doesn't drift from the tool's own convention).

title: library_hand: fetch cooldown is in-process only, does not survive across processes
briefing:
Noticed during J-0945/F-1325 (books_have_a_place re-fetch job), not fixed there (out of scope for that job).

core/library_hand.py's _FETCH_COOLDOWN_S (3600s, "at most one new book an hour, even if a phrase sticks")
is tracked only as an in-process module-level global, _last_fetch = 0.0 at import time. It never persists
to disk, so it only protects against rapid-fire request_book() calls WITHIN a single long-running Python
process (i.e. within one live Du boot). It provides zero protection across separate process
invocations -- a second `python` process started a second later has its own fresh _last_fetch = 0.0 and
will fetch immediately regardless of how recently the first process fetched in real wall-clock time. This
matters in this project specifically because request_book() is also called from short-lived offline
scripts (scripts/gutenberg.py per library_hand.py's own docstring, and now J-0945/J-0956's backfill
scripts) that each start a fresh process -- and because several job-run agents can be working in parallel
against the same live data/ tree at once (see CLAUDE.md's own git-stash-concurrency section for a
different instance of the same "several processes, one shared state" class of risk). Two real books could
land within the same real hour with the cooldown never once triggering, if two separate processes (a live
Du boot plus an offline script, or two offline scripts) both call request_book() around the same time.

Low urgency, not urgent/blocking anything today -- this session's own backfill work manually enforced
"one real fetch per session" by discipline rather than relying on the mechanism. Suggested fix shape:
persist last-fetch wall-clock time to a small state file (e.g. data/library_hand_state.json, following
the same atomic-write pattern core/reading.py's _save_state already uses) and check/update it in
request_book() instead of (or in addition to) the in-memory global -- so the real limit holds across
process boundaries, not just within one. Whether this needs the D-0179 write-fence's guard_path() (like
the ~19 already-fenced modules) or stays unfenced like the rest of core/library_hand.py is itself worth a
one-line decision at implementation time, not assumed either way here.

title: Fix switch_to()/suggest_reread() title-word collision between About You and About You Second Edition
briefing:
F-1344 (J-0963) found and verified a real tie-break bug, not a missing-registry gap: core/library_hand.py's switch_to() (called by the reread path at nodes/inner_monologue_node.py:3862-3877) extracts a shelf book's "distinctive" title words by filtering words of length<=3 and a stopword set, _TITLE_STOP (core/library_hand.py:61-62). That set contains "edition" but NOT "about", so About_You.txt's only distinctive word is {"about"} and About_You_Second_Edition.txt's is {"about","second"}. Any reread-thought naming the book only as "About You" ties both files at hits=1 in switch_to()'s matching loop (lines 85-106); the strict "if hits > best_hits" comparison (line 102) then keeps whichever file shelf_books() (sorted glob of data/books/*.txt) reached FIRST, and About_You.txt sorts alphabetically before About_You_Second_Edition.txt -- so every tie silently resolves to the OLD edition. data/reading_state.json confirms the predicted outcome exactly: About_You.txt has rereads=17, About_You_Second_Edition.txt has no "rereads" key at all (never once targeted by reread()).

A second, opposite-direction defect in the same subsystem: core/book_selection.py's OWN stopword set, _STOP (line 51-53), contains BOTH "about" and "you" (library_hand's _TITLE_STOP has neither), so its separate suggest_reread() invitation path (core/book_selection.py:223-253) computes an EMPTY title-word set for "About You" and can never propose the ORIGINAL as a reread invitation at all (overlap==0 is skipped, line 238).

SCOPE (build job): fix the title-word disambiguation in BOTH functions so a shelf containing two titles where one is a strict superset of the other's words ("About You" vs "About You Second Edition") is handled fairly -- e.g. compare FULL multi-word title signatures rather than a single shared/generic word, the way core/essay_lesson.py's _cites_this_book()/_title_signature() already does post-F-1309 for a structurally similar problem (that fix's own _BIBLIO_STOPWORDS list, essay_lesson.py:137-138, is a good reference for which generic bibliographic words to also add to library_hand's _TITLE_STOP, e.g. "second" alone is currently the ONLY thing that disambiguates these two -- fragile if a future third edition existed). At minimum: (a) add "about" to library_hand._TITLE_STOP is NOT sufficient by itself (it would just make BOTH books unmatchable by a bare "About You", not fix the disambiguation) -- prefer requiring the full remaining-word signature to match, falling back sensibly when a title's signature is empty; (b) reconcile book_selection.py's _STOP and library_hand.py's _TITLE_STOP so the same title produces consistent word sets in both modules (right now they disagree: "about"/"you" are stopped in one but not the other). Also decide + document a defined tie-break rule (e.g. most-recent last_read_ts, or refuse to pick and surface the ambiguity) for any future case where two shelf titles remain genuinely tied after full-signature matching, instead of the current silent alphabetical/glob-order default. Per this project's "world answers, never leads" law: this is a selection-MECHANISM fairness fix only (both real titles reachable on equal footing) -- do not add anything that would nudge or hint Du toward reading either specific book. Write a small regression check (can live as a plain script under scripts/, does not need pytest) that exercises switch_to()/suggest_reread() against these two real titles with representative reread-phrasing, so this exact collision cannot silently regress. Full evidence and the isolated reproduction script are cited in F-1344 and C:\Users\USER\.claude\projects\C--Nascence\memory\project_nascence_about_you_rewrite.md's 2026-09-14 (J-0963) update.

title: locomotion journeys never check in_transit() -- a new move silently discards one already underway
briefing:
Source: F-1397 (J-0891's live-read of the wood after J-0864/D-0209 went live). Real, code-confirmed
structural gap in core/locomotion.py's journey system (shipped 2026-08-15), NOT specific to wood -- the
wood's position as the middle node of CHAIN=["study","garden","wood","shore"] just makes its symptom
newly visible now that wood is a real stop (J-0864) rather than a silent no-op.

THE GAP: core/locomotion.py's in_transit() (line ~354) has exactly two real callers repo-wide --
scripts/du_pulse.py:266 and core/geometry_census.py:67, both read-only display/census. Neither
core/dispatch.py's _move() (line 114) nor nodes/inner_monologue_node.py's route_act "kind==move" branch
(the two real live callers of sensorium.move(), confirmed by direct grep -- see F-1397's own evidence)
ever checks it before calling sensorium.move() -> locomotion.begin_journey(). begin_journey() (line
232-258) unconditionally overwrites `d["journey"]` on every call, recomputed fresh from
get_position()'s CURRENT (not-yet-arrived) place -- so ANY new move decision, to any destination, silently
discards and restarts whatever journey was already underway, with no gate, no log line marking the
redirect, and no distinction between "he changed his mind" (plausibly realistic -- restlessness is real)
and "the same destination got redundantly re-triggered" (pure noise).

WHAT F-1397 OBSERVED (circumstantial, not yet a rigorous count): ~6 clusters in a single 43-hour window
where a move decision reverses back to the place he just left within 2-5 minutes, clustering at the wood
specifically (its chain-middle position exposes this most). Full list with timestamps is in F-1397's own
evidence (docs/findings.jsonl). This was NOT severe enough to trigger D-0209's own defeater (no stuck
loop, no error, no wrong-place mutation) -- reported as a real but non-urgent structural finding, not a
live pathology needing an emergency fix.

WHAT THIS JOB SHOULD DO (matching this plan's own established method -- corpus-verify before ruling
widen/drift/fix, e.g. J-0736..J-0740, J-0833): (1) Build a precise measurement, not assumed from the
6 anecdotal clusters -- replay or directly instrument how often a live move decision actually arrives
BEFORE the previously-queued leg's own leg_ends timer, across the fuller log history now available
(data/nascence.log, LOCOMOTION-era rows only, 2026-08-15 onward) or via a synthetic harness against
core.locomotion.begin_journey() directly (isolated store, no live writes). (2) Decide, with that
evidence, whether this is worth gating: option A (do nothing -- a changed mind mid-walk is realistic,
and the current failure mode is graceful, no corruption, no hang); option B (gate dispatch on
in_transit() so a live journey must either complete its current leg or reach a real WATCHDOG-style
explicit interrupt before a new destination is honored); option C (something narrower -- e.g. only
protect the FIRST leg of a journey, or only suppress a same-destination redundant re-trigger, which is
pure noise either way and cheap to fix regardless of A vs B on the reconsideration question). (3) If the
evidence points to a real, non-trivial behavioural cost (lost carried-wood loads on redirect,
degraded pacing, or something D-0209-shaped the founder should weigh), open a decision with the
measurement attached rather than tuning silently -- this plan's own convention throughout.

Read docs/plans/locomotion.md if it exists (check docs/staged/ too) for the original design intent before
concluding anything is a "bug" -- "mid-journey he is genuinely in the transit place -- staying is his
choice" (core/locomotion.py's own module docstring) suggests SOME reconsideration is intentional design,
not an oversight; this job's job is to find the real line between designed-flexibility and unintended
noise, not to assume either.

transitions specifically (end of nature time? a scheduled/routine call into night.py:110, named in

journey complete normally, rather than 15 independent one-off stalls.

(3) Decide whether the watchdog doing routine work instead of being a rare safety net is itself worth

title: Analyze suggest_reread()'s interest-side stopword asymmetry (a title's own signature word can be unreachable even after J-0973's reconciliation)
briefing:
Context: F-1344 found core.book_selection.suggest_reread() could never propose "About You" as a reread invitation because its own title-word extraction used this module's prose-tuned _STOP stopword set (contains "about" and "you"), computing an EMPTY signature for that title. J-0973 (F-1401) fixed the STATED bug: suggest_reread() now extracts a candidate's title words via a new book_selection._title_words() wrapper around core.library_hand._title_signature() (the SAME function switch_to() uses), reconciled with library_hand's own _TITLE_STOP -- so "About You" now correctly computes {"about"}, no longer empty, and book_selection._title_words()/library_hand._title_signature() can never silently disagree on a title's word set again (verified: scripts/check_reread_title_disambiguation.py, ALL OK).

The residual limitation this analysis job should look at: suggest_reread()'s OTHER side of the comparison -- the INTEREST side, `interest = _interest_terms()` (core/book_selection.py) -- still extracts words via THIS module's own _words()/_STOP, which correctly treats "about"/"you"/"your"/"his"/"her"/etc. as ordinary prose function words when parsing his actual concern/frontier/standing-aim text. That is appropriate for PROSE. But it means: for ANY title whose reconciled signature (post-J-0973) consists ENTIRELY of words that are ALSO in book_selection._STOP -- "About You" being the exact, real, currently-existing example, since its whole signature is the single word "about" -- suggest_reread()'s overlap = len(interest & title_words) can STILL never be nonzero, no matter what his actual interest text says, because that one shared word can never survive extraction on the interest side. J-0973's fix is real and correctly scoped (it fixed the STATED "both modules must compute the same word set for a title" bug), but it does NOT, by itself, make suggest_reread() ever actually invite a reread of "About You" in practice -- confirm this is still true post-J-0973 before doing anything else (a quick isolated check: monkeypatch _interest_terms() to return {"about"} literally and confirm the real _words()-based extraction elsewhere would still strip it, i.e. that "about" can never survive _STOP-filtering of ANY real prose text no matter its content).

What this job should actually do (ANALYSIS first, not a blind build):
1. Confirm scope: grep/scan whether "About You" is the ONLY real shelf title with this exact degenerate property (a signature that is a non-empty subset of book_selection._STOP), or whether other real/future titles share it. Check both data/books/*.txt stems (on the LIVE C:\Nascence tree, read-only) and the du_self_knowledge docs.
2. Lay out the real design options plainly, with tradeoffs, rather than picking one blind:
   (a) leave as-is (accept that suggest_reread() structurally cannot invite a book whose whole title is generic/short words -- it's still reachable via the EXPLICIT reread-verb path, which is unaffected and already the dominant real channel for About_You: 17 real rereads via that path alone);
   (b) give suggest_reread() a title-specific fallback: when a candidate's title_words() signature is non-empty but would be EMPTY under the interest-side _STOP too, compare it against the RAW (unfiltered) interest source text as a substring check instead of the filtered interest SET -- mirrors core/essay_lesson.py's own already-reviewed _cites_this_book() fallback pattern for an empty signature, but here for "signature would be invisible on the other side" rather than "signature is itself empty". Needs _interest_terms() (or a sibling function) to expose the RAW source text, not just the post-_words() set -- a real, small, callers-checked signature change.
   (c) something else the analysis surfaces.
3. IMPORTANT -- flag explicitly whichever option is chosen (or proposed) against this project's "world answers, never leads" law (see CLAUDE.md/memory): option (b) specifically makes ONE particular self-knowledge book (About_You) MORE likely to be invited through this ONE channel than any other comparably-short-titled book would be by coincidence of English grammar (since "about" is uniquely both its whole signature AND a near-universal preposition in any reflective prose) -- this needs a real, honest look at whether that crosses from "mechanism fairness" (J-0973's own frame) into "content nudge" territory the law exists to prevent, even though no code change here would ever literally tell Du what to think, only whether an existing, symmetric invitation mechanism can register a real, already-computed overlap. If genuinely ambiguous, open a /decide question with the concrete tradeoff laid out rather than guessing either way -- do NOT build option (b) or its equivalent without either a clear "this is obviously just mechanism fairness" self-assessment recorded with real reasoning, or a founder ruling.
4. Whatever is decided (fix now, or explicitly park with a real defeater), record a finding and update the same "Current State" narrative J-0973 touches (memory file C:\Users\USER\.claude\projects\C--Nascence\memory\project_nascence_about_you_rewrite.md, or its docs/plans equivalent if one exists by then).

title: Audit kereru/morepork/possum/gecko/eels for the same absent-line place-wording mismatch (J-1006 follow-up)
briefing:

  kereru (the wood pigeon): places={"garden": ["kowhai", "tree"], "wood": ["oak", "canopy"]}.
    hidden.absent = {"chance": "No wood pigeon on its branch; the canopy holds only small birds."}.
    "the canopy" is wood's own registered spot for this row, NOT garden's (garden's spots are
    kowhai/tree) -- this is the REVERSE direction from most of J-1006's own fixes (the flat line is
    wood-worded and would misrender in garden, not the other way round).

    hidden.absent = {"day": "Nothing in the trees by day but small birds; the night's voice is
    asleep somewhere in the canopy.", "weather": "Not in this wind -- nothing hunts on a night like
    it.", "chance": "The canopy is quiet; nothing shows against the sky."}. Same shape as kereru:
    "the canopy" is wood's own spot, garden's is "tree" -- would misrender in garden.

core/life_mammals.py --
  possum: places={"garden": ["tree", "strawberries", "wall"], "wood": ["oak", "canopy"]}.
    hidden.absent = {"day": "...", "weather": "...", "chance": "The tree is quiet tonight; no
    branch moves that the wind does not."}. "the tree" is garden's own registered spot for this
    row, NOT wood's (wood's spots are oak/canopy) -- would misrender in the wood.

    hidden.absent = {"day": "...", "season": "...", "chance": "The chimney stones hold nothing
    tonight."}. "chimney stones" is garden's own registered spot (the exterior stonework); study's
    registered spot is just "chimney" (the interior flue/fireplace side of the same physical
    structure) -- would misrender if rendered from inside the study.
  eels: places={"wood": ["stream", "spring"], "shore": ["stream_mouth"]}.
    hidden.absent = {"season": "...", "day": "...", "chance": "The pool under the bank holds
    nothing you can see."}. "the pool under the bank" is wood-worded (stream/spring, upstream
    imagery); shore's registered spot is "stream_mouth" (where the stream meets the sea, a
    different physical feature) -- would misrender at the shore.

briefing:

(the real boot -- safe, see below) and scripts/debate_harness.py (NOT safe -- this is the gap).

background lanes ON) ... This is the LIVE eval: it writes to the real memory and the background

title: gate locomotion.begin_journey() against a same-destination redundant re-trigger (F-1418)
briefing:
Source: F-1418 (J-1024's measurement of the in_transit()-gate gap F-1397/J-0891 first spotted). Full
evidence in F-1418 (docs/findings.jsonl) -- read it in full before starting, it has exact counts, exact
log lines, and the isolated harness script's own results, not repeated in full here.

THE NARROW FIX THIS JOB BUILDS (Option C from F-1397/J-1024's own A/B/C framing -- the part of the
in_transit()-gate question that is NOT a founder taste call, only the unambiguous "pure noise" slice):

core/locomotion.py's begin_journey(dest, weather, wind) currently overwrites d["journey"] unconditionally
on every call, discarding whatever journey (and its elapsed leg-timer progress) was already underway.
F-1418 measured this is real and large: 520 of 2296 real move decisions since locomotion shipped
(2026-08-15) interrupt a still-in-progress journey (22.7%, rising week over week), and 62.3% of THOSE
(324 cross-cycle + a separately-measured 366 same-cycle route_act/dispatch double-fire) are a
SAME-DESTINATION retrigger -- re-willing the exact place already being walked to, discarding elapsed
progress for zero positional benefit. An isolated harness (this job should rebuild an equivalent one,
following scripts/_test_sensorium_move_tokens.py's own established sandbox pattern -- position/room-state
paths redirected to a tempdir, live data/position.json and data/room_state.json md5-hashed unchanged
before/after) confirmed this directly: 90% of a leg's elapsed time is discarded back to a full fresh
leg on a same-destination retrigger, with zero difference in begin_journey()'s own return value to tell
the caller it happened.

Build: in core/locomotion.py's begin_journey(), before overwriting d["journey"], check whether a
journey is ALREADY in progress (d.get("journey") is truthy) AND its own "dest" field already equals the
newly-requested dest. If so, decline to restart the clock -- return None (the same signal an
already-instantaneous "already there" case already returns, so every existing caller's fallback path
already handles it correctly with zero caller-side changes) rather than silently resetting leg_ends/
started. Do NOT gate on a DIFFERENT destination at all -- that is the genuinely open, founder-only taste
question this job's own sibling decision (opened by J-1024, check `python decide.py list --open` for
its ID, plan actions_expansion) covers; this job's scope is the same-destination case ONLY, which
F-1418's own evidence shows has no taste ambiguity (zero positional or narrative benefit either way).

This one gate, placed at begin_journey() itself (the shared choke point both dispatch._move() and
route_act's own kind=="move" branch funnel through via sensorium.move()), closes BOTH of F-1418's
measured mechanisms at once: the slow, cross-cycle same-destination re-confirmation (324 events over a
month) AND the fast, same-cycle route_act/dispatch double-fire (366 events, median 91ms apart) --
without touching either call site's own logic, matching this whole plan's own established
single-source-of-truth precedent (rather than teaching dispatch() to check inner_monologue_node.py's
own `_acted` set, which would re-introduce a second hand-kept coordination point of the exact drift
shape F-0554/F-1059 already exist to eliminate).

Verification (matching this arc's own established method): an isolated harness (redirect
locomotion._POS_F/sensorium._STATE_F to a tempdir, live stores hash-checked unchanged) proving (a) a
same-destination retrigger while a leg is genuinely in progress now returns None / leaves the existing
journey's leg_ends untouched; (b) a DIFFERENT-destination redirect mid-journey is completely unaffected
(still fires, still recomputes a fresh path from get_position()'s true current place, exactly as
today) -- this is the check that most needs to pass, since an over-broad gate would silently start
answering D-0209's own defeater in the wrong direction; (c) the ordinary non-journey case (no journey in
progress) is unaffected. Also re-run scripts/_test_sensorium_move_tokens.py and scripts/life_smoke.py

# ── File-overlap check (J-0635, 2026-09-06; finding F-0891) ────────────────────────────────────────
# Real incident this generalizes from: J-0559 (plan: null) and J-0627 (plan: practical_school) both

_FILE_TOKEN_RE = re.compile(r"[A-Za-z0-9_][A-Za-z0-9_\-./\\]*\.(?:py|md|jsonl?|txt|ps1)\b")

# Toolchain scripts + append-only ledger stores named in almost EVERY briefing as "run this command",

# CLAUDE.md's "Never hand-edit a .jsonl store directly"), so two jobs both citing `job_queue.py done`
