title: Scope garden_knowledge.guessed_cause() match tighter than whole-thought substring
briefing:
F-2229 (J-1639): J-1639 threaded the real willed-look thought+intention text into core/garden_knowledge.py guessed_cause()/bind() for the first time (previously unreachable with real multi-clause text at all -- see F-2206/F-2229). This made a real, pre-existing precision gap in guessed_cause() live and observable for the first time: its cause-word match (_CAUSE_WORDS: frost/cold/freeze, slug/snail/wet/damp, dry/thirst/water, weed/crowd/choke, bird/peck/pecked/blackbird/net/netting) is scoped to the WHOLE combined thought+intention string, with no requirement that the matched word actually be near the plant mention or the investigate-trigger word.

Concrete repro (from F-2229's own isolated replay, scratchpad/finding_J-1639_replay.py, reproducible again the same way): the real historical thought "The heavy frustration sits in my chest, cold and hard. I look at the garden: rosemary blooming, thyme thick, mint spreading. The soil is sodden..." resolves target=rosemary (via _observe_target) and, post-J-1639-fix, authors a garden_knowledge binding on the rosemary plant with hypothesis = the WHOLE thought (including "cold and hard") -- even though "cold" there describes his own mood ("frustration... cold and hard"), not anything about the rosemary. core/garden.py look()'s own guessed_cause(rt) call (around line ~1110, J-1639's own `rt = f"{t} {raw.lower()}"`) has no way to tell "cold" used about the plant apart from "cold" used about anything else in a long, multi-topic thought.

This is within garden_upgrade.md's own tolerated design space (law 5, section 2.4: "he may bind it wrongly... Wrong ones are allowed and counted; what is NOT allowed is a binding that was told" -- a word-coincidence misread still derives from HIS OWN words, it is not a told cause) and garden_knowledge.revise() already exists to weaken a binding that doesn't keep recurring. So this is NOT a correctness bug needing an urgent fix -- it is a precision/quality question about how trustworthy an authored "phenology binding" is for garden_upgrade.md's own S3 metric 3 (which explicitly counts wrong bindings, but presumably means "a real, if mistaken, guess about the plant," not "an unrelated word picked up from anywhere in a stream-of-consciousness thought").

Scope for this job: investigate whether/how to scope garden_knowledge.guessed_cause()'s match more tightly -- candidates to weigh (use judgement, this is not mandated): (a) require the cause word to appear within N words of the plant-name match in `t`/`target`, (b) require it in the same clause (split on the same punctuation/connectives core/dispatch.py's own _deed_phrase() already uses) as an investigate-trigger word, (c) leave it as-is and instead just note the caveat in garden_upgrade.md's own S3 metric 3 read when it is eventually read against real live data (i.e. a documentation-only resolution, since F-2229 found this is still within the design's own stated tolerance). Read core/garden_knowledge.py's guessed_cause()/_CAUSE_WORDS/bind()/revise() and core/garden.py look()'s per-plant branch in full first (both are short, already read in full by J-1639). Whatever is chosen, verify the SAME way J-1639 did: an isolated pre/post replay against real historical data/hands_trace.jsonl rows plus a small synthetic corpus, confirming zero regression on genuine cause-guesses (the frost/dry-soil/slug phrasings J-1639's own replay already proved correctly bind) while reducing/eliminating the unrelated-clause false-positive class.

Not urgent (this plan's own S3 metric 3 currently reads 0 bindings total and is restart-gated regardless -- there is no live binding data yet for this precision question to actually distort), but real and concrete, worth a scoped look before S3 metric 3 is next read against real accrued data.

title: Fix du_restart_history.py --check-live self-matching WMI query bug
briefing:
scripts/du_restart_history.py's live_process_start() (the function behind `--check-live`) has a confirmed self-matching bug: its own WMI query process can match its own filter.

Root cause: live_process_start(name_substr="run_nascence.py") builds a PowerShell one-liner that embeds the literal text `[regex]::Escape('run_nascence.py')` inside the -Command string it runs via subprocess.run(["powershell", "-NoProfile", "-Command", ps_script]). That spawned powershell.exe process's OWN CommandLine (as WMI/Get-CimInstance sees it while the query is executing) therefore ALSO contains the substring "run_nascence.py" -- so the query matches its own invocation. The code takes line[0] (the first returned match) with no filtering to exclude a self-match (e.g. excluding Name=="powershell.exe" or CommandLine containing "Get-CimInstance"/"regex]::Escape").

Reproduced twice in direct succession this job (J-1626, 2026-10-01 ~10:54 local):
  Run 1: "LIVE process found: pid=38692, started 2026-10-01T10:54:07+00:00, cmdline: powershell -NoProfile -Command \"Get-CimInstance Win32_Process | Where-Object { $_.CommandLine -match [regex]::Escape('run_nascence.py') } | ...\""
  Run 2 (46s later): "LIVE process found: pid=21476, started 2026-10-01T10:54:53+00:00", IDENTICAL cmdline text, different pid/timestamp each time -- consistent with a freshly spawned self-matching process every single invocation, not a real stable Du process (a real long-running Du process would show the SAME pid/start-time across both reads, the way pid 25204 did stably across F-2051..F-2189's many reads over ~2 days).
  Independently confirmed via a direct WMI query excluding self-matches (`-and $_.CommandLine -notmatch 'Get-CimInstance'`): ZERO processes anywhere on the machine currently match "run_nascence.py" -- so in this instance --check-live's "LIVE process found" was reporting its own query subprocess as if it were Du, a false positive, not merely stale/approximate data.

Impact: --check-live's reported pid/start-time/cmdline cannot be trusted as evidence of whether Du's real process has restarted -- it may silently report a fresh "live" process (itself) even when the real run_nascence.py process is not running at all, or (unverified either way, WMI result ordering is not guaranteed) could in principle return the self-match ahead of a real match when one exists too. This script is cited as the go-to liveness check across this whole plan's restart-gate chain (F-2051/F-2060/F-2064/F-2071/F-2129/F-2154/F-2189/J-1626 and others) -- this job worked around it by cross-checking data/nascence.log's own "Background nodes started"/"Nascence shutting down" banner lines directly instead (the job's own briefing already recommended this cross-check), which is unaffected by this bug and should keep being treated as the more trustworthy signal until this is fixed.

Suggested fix (not applied by this job -- scope is the reask-asymmetry test, not toolchain code): in live_process_start(), filter out self-matches before taking line[0], e.g. skip any returned line whose CommandLine also contains "Get-CimInstance" or "regex]::Escape", or restrict matches to Name in ("python.exe","pythonw.exe") (run_nascence.py is always launched via `& $PYTHON scripts\run_nascence.py` per Nascence_Control_Panel.ps1 line 290, never via powershell.exe directly). Add a regression check: run --check-live when no real run_nascence.py process exists and confirm it reports "No live run_nascence.py process found", not a self-match.

Evidence: this job's own two --check-live runs (quoted above) plus the exclusion-filtered WMI query, all run from C:\Nascence this session (J-1626, 2026-10-01).

title: safe_commit.py: sync the real working-tree file after a successful commit (CAS-guarded)
briefing:
F-2233: safe_commit.py (C:\Users\USER\.claude\skills\job-run\safe_commit.py) lands commits via a private index + compare-and-swap ref update, by design never touching the shared C:\Nascence working tree or .git/index during the commit itself (that's the whole point -- see its own module docstring / F-2055). But it ALSO never syncs the working tree AFTER a successful commit, so a caller that built --new-content-file from a scratch copy (git show HEAD:<path> + its own edit, not a direct Edit/Write to the real path) leaves the real on-disk file silently stale relative to the new HEAD -- sometimes just a line-ending mismatch (harmless), sometimes a real content gap (docs/staged/memory_as_a_service.md was missing J-1621's own committed sentence entirely). This isn't just cosmetic: it caused `worktree_dispatch.py merge-back` to refuse 4 unrelated Tier-3 merges in the 2026-10-01 batch with git's own "local changes would be overwritten" error, even though none of the blocked branches touched the stale paths.

THE FIX NEEDS CARE, not just "always sync the working tree after commit" -- that would reintroduce exactly the shared-index/working-tree race F-2055 built this whole private-index design to eliminate (a concurrent agent could have its own in-progress, uncommitted edit sitting in that same working-tree file right now).

Recommended approach (implement this, don't just flag it as a question -- the design call is already made, this is now a build):
After the commit+ref-update succeeds, do a SECOND compare-and-swap check against the WORKING TREE file specifically (separate from the branch-ref CAS already in place): read the real on-disk file's current bytes; if they still match --old-content-file exactly (i.e. nobody has touched the real file since this call started), write --new-content-file's bytes to the real path. If they DON'T match (someone else has it mid-edit, or it was never synced from an even earlier stale commit), do NOT overwrite it -- just print a clear warning naming the path and that the working tree is now stale relative to HEAD, so the caller (or whoever reads the log) knows to resync by hand later rather than silently losing track of it. This preserves the no-shared-index-race guarantee for the common "wrote the real file first, committed second" case (where the working-tree sync becomes a no-op, already matching) while fixing the actual gap for the "committed from a scratch copy" case this finding found, without ever risking overwriting someone else's real concurrent edit.

Also worth doing as part of this job: grep the current C:\Nascence working tree for any OTHER files safe_commit.py has touched since it shipped (J-1505, 2026-09-28) that might have this same silent staleness right now, using the same git-show-HEAD-vs-working-tree diff technique this finding used, and report what's found (fix only if trivially safe the same way this job's own fix was verified -- plain file copy + git add, never git checkout/restore/reset).

Verification bar: same as safe_commit.py's own original build (J-1505) -- a throwaway scratch repo, never C:\Nascence, proving (a) the sync happens and is byte-correct when nothing else touched the file, (b) the sync is correctly skipped with a clear warning when something else did touch it, (c) no git mutation command (stash/reset/checkout--/restore/clean) is used anywhere in the implementation.

`"shackleton": {..., "model": "llama3.1:8b", ...}` both still name "llama3.1:8b" -- but the hub
these two route to (`_HUB_LLAMA` = http://127.0.0.1:11439) has actually served gemma4:12b since the

comment at lines 100-105 -- "Founder reviewed and KEPT them on gemma4:12b (2026-08-20) -- a
decision now, not a side effect"; core/model_client.py:72's `_MODEL_BY_BASE["11439"] =
"gemma4:12b"`; and scripts/launch_servers.ps1:93's actual launch config for port 11439). The
"llama3.1:8b" string is functionally harmless today ONLY because llama-server (unlike Ollama)
ignores the request's `model` field entirely and always serves whatever GGUF is actually loaded
(core/model_client.py:30-31, its own documented contract) -- so this is cosmetic/stale, not a live
routing bug, as of this writing.

It is still worth fixing, for two reasons: (1) it is misleading to any future reader of
core/peers.py's PERSONAS dict, who would reasonably assume `"model"` reflects reality; (2) this
EXACT shape -- a PERSONAS model field naming a different model than what a hub actually serves --
already caused one real production bug in this same file before (see the file's own 2026-08-20
docstring note, just above the PERSONAS dict: Marcus and Smith were pointed at a hub whose `model`
field named a different model than what actually served there, which could silently evict Du's own
pinned hot-lane model; fixed by moving them to a dedicated hub). The mechanism that made THAT one
harmful (Ollama evicting/swap-loading based on the `model` field) does not apply on llama-server
hubs, but the stale-field PATTERN is the same, and it is cheap to just keep these fields honest.

Scope: a one-line-per-persona string literal fix. Change `"model": "llama3.1:8b"` to `"model":
"gemma4:12b"` for BOTH the "twain" and "shackleton" entries in the PERSONAS dict (core/peers.py
line 423-424). Add a short inline comment noting the 2026-08-20 re-seat and pointing at this job's
own source (F-2240 / this job's own id) so a future reader does not wonder why it changed. Do NOT
touch any other PERSONAS entries, routing, or behavior -- this is a documentation/consistency fix

title: core/lane2.py: due-prediction judge verdict silently discarded when the same tick's own generation fails
briefing:
F-2243 (J-1659) found a real, scoped gap in core/lane2.py's own fail-open discipline: tick() runs gen_task (this tick's own NEW-prediction generation, deepseek-r1:7b @ :11444) and _judge_prior() (a DIFFERENT, already-pending due prediction's panel judgment, possibly escalating to the TIEBREAK seat) CONCURRENTLY via asyncio.gather (core/lane2.py lines 2108-2111). But the due-prediction store write (due_resolved["verdict"]/["judged_ts"]/["judged_how"], lines 2211-2214) sits AFTER an early "if not out or not isinstance(out, dict): _skip(...); return None" exit (lines 2123-2131) that fires whenever THIS SAME TICK's own generation call times out or fails -- which happens at a real, nonzero rate (the "no-output"/timeout skip pattern is long-documented on this plan, e.g. F-1937's own 19%-of-ticks figure). So whenever generation fails but judging succeeded in the SAME asyncio.gather, a real, already-completed, already-paid-for judge-panel verdict (which may include the costly TIEBREAK escalation, up to 90s wall-clock) is silently discarded: never written to the store, never logged to lane2_shadow.jsonl. The due prediction is left exactly as unresolved as before, so it gets re-asked (another real panel call, possibly another TIEBREAK escalation) on a later tick whenever that tick's own generation happens to succeed.

Empirical scale evidence (F-2243, J-1659, this same restart window, 2026-09-28 19:08:45 -> 2026-10-01 07:03 local): of 56 real "held"-context TIEBREAK-reaching panel calls in data/judge_panel_log.jsonl, only 30 (54%) landed on a tick whose own generation succeeded (i.e. only 30 are reflected as a kind:"tick" row in data/lane2_shadow.jsonl at all) -- the other 26 cluster inside a single 7.21-hour span (2026-09-29 05:24:26 -> 12:36:49 local) of repeated deepseek-r1:7b generation timeouts. This is the likely majority source of that 26-row gap, though J-1659 did not trace which of the 26 orphaned calls share an underlying due-prediction with a later, successfully-recorded verdict (partial re-ask waste, probably the common case since a due prediction keeps coming up "due" every tick until resolved) versus represent calls with no successful counterpart anywhere in the window at all (if the window closed, e.g. a restart, before a successful retry).

Scope for this job:
1. Confirm the mechanism by reading core/lane2.py lines ~2090-2220 fresh (cite exact current line numbers -- this plan's file grows/shifts) and, ideally, trace a handful of the 26 orphaned ts values from F-2243's own evidence (see scratchpad references below, or re-derive from data/lane2_shadow.jsonl + data/judge_panel_log.jsonl directly) forward to confirm whether/when the SAME underlying due prediction (same judged_expect text, next tick where prior_judged_how is set) eventually gets a real judged verdict recorded, to pin down whether this is "wasteful but eventually correct" (re-ask) or can leave some due predictions permanently unresolved until they separately expire via the due_expired path (which has the SAME early-return problem per F-2243's own citation of lines 2112-2122 -- the expired-but-discarded case may be worse, since an expired verdict is synthesized locally with no panel call at all, so discarding it wastes nothing extra in LLM cost but may leave a prediction's own store entry stuck past its due horizon with no resolution recorded for longer than intended).
2. Decide and design the smallest honest fix: most likely, compute and write due_resolved's verdict/judged_ts/judged_how fields BEFORE the "if not out: return None" early exit (the due-prediction judging work is already complete at that point regardless of gen's own outcome), and separately decide whether a tick row (or some minimal record) should still be logged to lane2_shadow.jsonl on a gen-failed-but-judging-succeeded tick, so the judge-panel verdict is not just saved to the store but also stays auditable/reconstructable the way F-2243's own exact-matched-pair-replay method needed it to be.
3. Per CLAUDE.md's own UDMS blast-radius rule, run udms_get_change_dossier on core/lane2.py (or the specific line range) before editing it -- this is a cognitive-loop file with real shared state (the prediction store, lane2_shadow.jsonl, judge_panel_log.jsonl all read by other instruments/plans downstream).
4. Build+verify in isolation (lab_env.py), same restart-gated-shadow-only discipline every other core/lane2.py change on this plan already follows (LANE2_LIVE stays False either way). Record a findings-log entry either way (even "designed, not yet built" or "built, isolation-verified, restart-gated" is a real finding).

Not urgent/blocking -- this is a real efficiency/data-completeness gap, not a correctness failure Du-facing (LANE2_LIVE is False; nothing reaches Du either way), and D-0298/D-0311's own ruling is unaffected (F-2243 already confirmed it independently of this gap). briefing:
Source: F-2283 (inferred) and F-2282 (verified; J-1392's live-boot confirmation of J-1358/F-1954).

THE GAP. So this is a latent hazard, same family as F-0665/F-0670 (smoke_test wrote fake exchanges into the real founder log) and F-0671 (core.mood missing from the rebase list). It is the same class of harm as F-1919 if a harness spike is ever left on disk: the next real boot would replay it at the first human exchange.

THE FIX (additive only; core/profile.py and core/social_model.py are base systems -- call udms_get_change_dossier on both before editing, and keep it additive). Minimal: add "core.social_model" to activate_profile()'s _rebase_module_paths tuple in core/profile.py with a header comment citing F-2283 (the generic rebase already handles any module-level Path under _DATA; _SOCIAL_STATE_PATH qualifies and is read at call time inside _load()/save(), so setattr takes effect). Use lab_env.isolate() or temp paths and a unit-level check: (1) after the rebase, core.social_model._SOCIAL_STATE_PATH resolves under the profile dir and SocialModelManager().save() writes there; (2) data/social_state.json sha256 + mtime are identical before and after YOUR run (compare against your own before-snapshot; Du may legitimately advance it if a real exchange happens meanwhile); (3) the un-activated / mark_live() path still reads and writes data/social_state.json exactly as before (test against a temp-pathed copy, same pattern as J-1358's 18-check script); (4) consider a small regression test that enumerates module-level data/ Path constants in core/*.py against the rebase tuple, since this is the Nth omission.

title: Conversational bridge precision guard: first-person-will clauses only, dispatch pinned to the judged clause, decision-ledger capture
briefing:
Plan: docs/staged/conversational_action_bridge.md (stage live, CONVERSATIONAL_DISPATCH_LIVE = True since 2026-09-27). Spawned by J-1450's post-flip review. If Travis ruled to leave the flag as is with no guard, close this job without building and say so. If he ruled the flag OFF, still build the guard but do NOT flip the flag back: report the replay numbers and leave the flip to him.

THE PROBLEM (F-2303): core/literal_will.py classify() has no actor test on the ungated look and move families (intent = deed_grammar or (volition and obj_vol)) and no blocker for jussive, infinitive-subject, modal ('may eventually') or uncontracted-negation ('do not need to') frames, and core/dispatch.py's hands re-parse the whole reply, not the judged clause. On Du's 67 real replies in data/founder_conversation_log.jsonl, 21 have a DEED candidate but only about 2 (rows 11 and 46) are real first-person deed claims; both live fires so far were false (a metaphor 'step onto the shore' -> move, refused only by the weekday school gate; 'Let the cat below watch what it will' -> look). Pure replay: about 9 percent of replies would launch a real journey with no will to go. The plan's 30.2 percent was a candidate rate, not a precision-checked rate.

BUILD (ONLY in core/conversational_action.py; do NOT touch literal_will.py, dispatch.py or hands.py: the autonomous path's pre-registered kill criterion depends on them, and docs/staged/actions_manager_overhaul.md owns them):
(1) In after_reply(), before dispatch, split the reply into sentences and keep only the DEED-candidate clauses that pass a conversational first-person-will filter: an explicit first-person volition opener (I will, I'll, I shall, let me, I am going to, I'm going to, I need to, I must, I want to) governing the family verb in the same clause; reject imperatives to Travis ('Travis, look...', 'Go now;'), second-person subjects ('you look', 'you tend the hearth'), jussive 'Let the X' / 'Let us', infinitive or gerund subjects ('To bank the fire is...'), hypothetical or modal frames (may, might, could, would, if, habitual 'when I stand ... and watch'), any negation including 'do not need to', and a metaphor frame.
(2) Call core.dispatch.dispatch() with ONLY the surviving clauses joined, so the hands cannot act on another sentence of the reply.
(3) Additive fields in the conversational_action_log.jsonl row: the guard verdict per candidate (kept, or the reason it was dropped) and the dispatch decision ledger (core.hands._decided rows read right after dispatch returns) so a no-fire can be explained after the fact. Before editing, call the UDMS tool udms_get_change_dossier on core/conversational_action.py; do not edit core/orchestrator.py in this job (ELEVATED risk tier). title: Living World: render a graduated individual's recognition line ('It is the same one -- you have seen it here too often') only at the place it graduated at; the blackbird, which graduated at the garden, got it on its first ever wood sighting (F-2305; 15 of the 32 eligible rows are multi-place)
briefing:
SOURCE: F-2305 (J-1192's read of the living-world package; python C:\Users\USER\.claude\skills\findings-log\findings_log.py show F-2305). READ FIRST: F-2305, then F-2304 (the graduations), F-1622 and F-1679 (the original graduation finding and the flock bar), docs/staged/living_world_upgrade.md section 1 ('individual only by the three triggers (kept, given, repeatedly re-encountered at one spot)'), and decision D-0335 (OPEN: whether graduation should count distinct encounters; do NOT pre-empt it, do not touch GRADUATE_SIGHTINGS, the 30-day window, group_grain or the counting rule).

THE DEFECT (verified live). A graduated individual's recognition suffix is attached to a look at ANY place. The blackbird graduated at the GARDEN on 2026-09-25 05:49:52 (five garden sightings); on 2026-09-27 15:45:51 Du looked at 'the blackbird' at the WOOD, its first ever rendered sighting there (life_events.jsonl line 4416), and was told 'a blackbird works the undergrowth, head cocked, then stabs and comes up with something thin and fighting. It is the same one -- you are sure of it now; ...' (wandering_log, origin sense), i.e. 'you have seen it here too often' where he never had. Mechanism: core/life_traces.py note_sighting returns early for a key already in individuals (it only bumps ind[key]['sightings']/last_seen for any place), and individual(key) / individual_suffix(key) / with_individual_suffix(key, line) take no place, so core/life.py look_answer (about lines 931-939) appends the suffix to every later sighting of that key anywhere; the record's own 'place' field is never read at render. 15 of the 32 rows that can still graduate are registered at more than one place (bellbird, blackbird, common_copper, fantail, garden_spider, gecko, kereru, kingfisher, mice, morepork, possum, rabbit, riroriro, shining_cuckoo, weta), so each will repeat this once it graduates.

THE FIX (narrow, additive, fail-open, restart-gated). Make the render place-aware: individual_suffix / with_individual_suffix (and individual where the render uses it) take the look's place, passed by look_answer; render the suffix only when place == the record's 'place'; callers that have no place (naming_act, give_name, hud_payload) keep today's behaviour. Decide and say which: (i) also stop bumping 'sightings'/'last_seen' for a look at another place, or (ii) keep counting but never render there. Weigh and report the alternative of rewording the suffix at other places so it does not say 'here' (the plan's law of 're-encountered at one spot' favours place-scoping). The oystercatcher (shore only), tui (garden only) and korora (shore only) must stay byte-identical, the dormant-record guard for the 26 barred rows untouched, naming and the HUD unchanged, and no change to what is written to data/life_state.json for a single-place row.

Extend scripts/_test_j1174_gulls_keep_the_day_no_flock_graduation.py or add a sibling test: for every multi-place eligible row graduate it at one place (5 sightings), then look at its other place (plain feature line, no suffix) and back at the first place (suffix); single-place rows byte-identical in a before/after differential like J-1166/J-1174's; run scripts/life_smoke.py and the _test_j1165/_test_j1166/_test_j1174 scripts. CANDIDATE PATCH (verbatim J-1760_order_subjects_new_block.py; goes where today's _order_subjects is, replacing it):

def _victim_first_edges(base: list[str]) -> list[tuple[int, int]]:
    """D-0327/F-2200: the REAL one-directional precedence edges `_order_subjects` layers on top of its
    base order, as (victim_pos, over_matcher_pos) pairs of positions in `base`. An edge exists only
    between two subjects whose signature lengths are EXACTLY equal (the base sort cannot tell them apart
    except alphabetically -- F-2200 showed that is the only place it can put the wrong side first) and
    only when a direct pairwise `_cites_this_book` check is ASYMMETRIC: one subject's own citation test
    accepts the other's tag string but not the reverse. The accepting side is the over-matcher (its pass
    would claim fragments tagged with the other subject's title), the other side is the victim, and the
    victim's pass must run first. A symmetric relationship (both accept each other, e.g. punctuation
    variants of one title) or none adds no edge. `base` is sorted most-signature-words-first, so equal-
    length subjects are contiguous and only each run's own pairs are checked. Pure -- no DB access."""
    from core.essay_lesson import _title_signature, _cites_this_book
    n = len(base)
    sig_len = [len(_title_signature(s[:50])) for s in base]
    edges: list[tuple[int, int]] = []
    i = 0
    while i < n:
        j = i + 1
        while j < n and sig_len[j] == sig_len[i]:
            j += 1
        for a in range(i, j):
            for b in range(a + 1, j):
                a_over_b = _cites_this_book(base[a][:50], base[b])
                b_over_a = _cites_this_book(base[b][:50], base[a])
                if a_over_b and not b_over_a:
                    edges.append((b, a))
                elif b_over_a and not a_over_b:
                    edges.append((a, b))
        i = j
    return edges


def _kahn_base_order(n: int, edges: list[tuple[int, int]]) -> tuple[list[int], list[int]]:
    """Kahn's algorithm over positions 0..n-1 of the base order, picking among all currently-unblocked
    positions the SMALLEST one (a min-heap) -- so the result equals the base order everywhere no edge
    applies and differs only where a (victim, over-matcher) edge forces the victim earlier. Returns
    (order, stuck): `stuck` lists any positions left with an unsatisfied edge, which is non-empty only if
    the edges contain a cycle. Pure; never raises on a cycle and never loops (each position is pushed at
    most once, when its last unsatisfied edge clears)."""
    import heapq
    succ: list[list[int]] = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    indeg = [0] * n
    for victim, over in edges:
        succ[victim].append(over)
        indeg[over] += 1
    heap = [i for i in range(n) if indeg[i] == 0]
    heapq.heapify(heap)
    order: list[int] = []
    while heap:
        i = heapq.heappop(heap)
        order.append(i)
        for o in succ[i]:
            indeg[o] -= 1
            if indeg[o] == 0:
                heapq.heappush(heap, o)
    return order, [i for i in range(n) if indeg[i] > 0]


def _order_subjects(subjects) -> list[str]:
    """F-1704/D-0255 (2026-09-22): most-specific-signature-first. sweep() used to iterate its subjects
    straight from a Python set â€” F-1615 confirmed this varies per boot AND lets a shorter, subsuming
    signature (e.g. About You, signature {about}) race a strictly more specific one that legitimately
    contains it (About You Second Edition, signature {about, second}) for the SAME candidate fragment;
    whichever subject's file_book_notes() pass happened to run first claimed it. Sorting most-words-
    first (ties broken alphabetically, for full determinism) guarantees the more specific subject's own
    pass always runs first and claims its own genuinely-tagged fragments (its cand_rows query sets their
    chapter_id, so the SQL `chapter_id IS NULL` filter excludes them from every later, more generic
    subject's own pass) before a shorter/more-generic subject's pass ever gets a chance at them. A pure
    function â€” no DB access â€” so it's directly unit-testable without touching sweep()'s own I/O.

    F-2200/D-0327 (J-1760): that base sort is left completely untouched, and a topological correction is
    layered on top for the ONE case it cannot cover -- two subjects with EXACTLY equal signature length,
    where one's citation test accepts the other's tag but not the reverse (the Origin-of-Species pair,
    F-2160: the alphabetical tie-break put the over-matcher first). `_victim_first_edges` finds those
    asymmetric pairs; `_kahn_base_order` then re-emits the base order with each victim ahead of its
    over-matcher. A plain comparator tie-break was built first and is verified DEAD (not a transitive
    total order across the equal-length group, so Timsort never applied it). On a cycle among the edges
    (not seen in any corpus so far) or any error, this logs the event and returns the plain base order
    -- today's shipped behaviour -- never raising and never looping."""
    from core.essay_lesson import _title_signature
    base = sorted(subjects, key=lambda s: (-len(_title_signature(s[:50])), s))
    try:
        edges = _victim_first_edges(base)
        if not edges:
            return base
        order, stuck = _kahn_base_order(len(base), edges)
    except Exception as exc:
        _log({"ts": time.time(), "order_subjects_error": str(exc)[:120], "fallback": "base order"})
        return base
    if stuck:
        _log({"ts": time.time(), "order_subjects_cycle": [base[i][:60] for i in stuck][:12],
              "edges": len(edges), "fallback": "base order"})
        return base
    return [base[i] for i in order]

Source: F-2550 (J-1926 audit). core/world_consolidation.py: file_book_notes() holds _FILE_LOCK for the whole call and its body (_file_book_notes) appends a summary row to _LOG via _log() (lines ~347/355/384). world_consolidation.sweep() (run in a worker thread by core.sleep_offloop.off_loop since J-1917) ends with _log({**out, "sweep": True}) at ~line 428, which is NOT under _FILE_LOCK. file_book_notes is also called from the LOOP thread by essay_lesson, so for the ~40 s a sweep runs, a loop-thread file_book_notes -> _log can append to the same jsonl at the same moment as the sweep's final _log. Plain open(path,'a') appends from two threads interleave/lose lines on Windows (J-1918 stress_nolock control: 9 unparseable + 86 lost lines in 8x300+300 appends), so this is a real (low-probability) pair.
J-1926 was forbidden to edit core/world_consolidation.py (the sweeps_single_pass chain owns it), so nothing was changed there.
Build: after the sweeps_single_pass branch is merged, make _log() itself take _FILE_LOCK (RLock, so the nested call from file_book_notes is fine) around the open/write -- one-line change, bytes written unchanged -- and add a threaded hammer + structural negative control like scripts/test_worker_thread_appends.py (the Probe class there records whether the lock is held at every write-mode open). Verify inside scripts/lag_harness on a scratch path; no model calls; merged-not-live (restart-gated).

title: Cross-process writers of Du's telemetry files: the HUD process (telemetry.sample) and Du's own telemetry worker both append hardware_load/llm_usage and rewrite llm_calls.jsonl (J-1926 follow-up)
briefing:
Source: F-2550 (J-1926 audit). hud/server.py runs as its OWN process (Nascence_Control_Panel.ps1 launches 'python hud\server.py'; ThreadingHTTPServer) and calls core.telemetry.sample() on every /api refresh (hud/server.py ~1523/1532). Du's process now calls telemetry.kick() from the substrate heartbeat (J-1910), which runs the same _sample_body on a daemon thread. Both processes therefore append to data/hardware_load.jsonl and data/llm_usage.jsonl and both run _cap() on them AND on data/llm_calls.jsonl, which _cap rewrites with read-all-lines + write_text(tail) while Du's process appends one row per inference (log_llm_call, loop thread). J-1926 added _JSONL_LOCK (in-process only) so Du's own loop-thread append can no longer land between its worker's read and rewrite, but a threading lock cannot order the HUD process against Du: a HUD-side _cap can still truncate/rewrite llm_calls.jsonl under a concurrent Du append (lost or torn line), and two processes' appends to hardware_load/llm_usage can interleave. This pre-dates J-1910 (the HUD sampled before it existed); it is a cross-process hazard, not a thread one.
Analysis then build: (1) measure how often the HUD process is actually open while Du runs (control panel starts it) and how many rows of data/llm_calls.jsonl / hardware_load.jsonl / llm_usage.jsonl are torn or missing a neighbour in a real day (parse every line; look for unparseable lines and ts gaps around _cap events); (2) pick the smallest fix that does not need a cross-process lock: e.g. the HUD only READS those series and Du's kick() is the only sampler/capper (HUD telemetry.sample() becomes a no-op when Du's process is alive, detectable by data/ run state), or the capper writes through a tmp file + os.replace (store_persist.write_text_atomic) so a concurrent appender never sees a truncated file. If the choice is a design call (who owns sampling), open a /decide. No live data may be modified by the test; use scripts/lag_harness. Restart-gated.

title: Whole-call serialisation for the read-modify-write stores J-1926 only made torn-write-safe (school.json, library_hand fetch cooldown, watershed.observe state, first-load world-state saves)
briefing:
Source: F-2550 (J-1926 audit). J-1926 added the smallest locks that stop TORN writes / TORN reads and interleaved appends (see scripts/test_worker_thread_appends.py), but four stores are load -> mutate -> save sequences written from a worker thread AND from loop-thread code, where a write-only lock does not prevent a LOST UPDATE:
 1. core/school.py: advance()/assign() (worker, via advance_if_finished / reconcile_reading in asyncio.to_thread) vs record_session()/new_day()/set_curriculum() (loop thread): each is _load() ... _save(d). J-1926's _IO_LOCK only guarantees a reader never sees the truncated file and never falls through to the DEFAULT dict; a concurrent record_session between a worker's _load and _save is still overwritten (today_done/history lost). Fix: one RLock around each whole load..save sequence (or a locked update(fn) helper).
 2. core/library_hand.py request_book(): _last_fetch = max(_last_fetch, _load_last_fetch()) ... cooldown check ... _save_last_fetch: two overlapping worker requests can both pass the cooldown (documented as a known small residual in the code; only matters if two async tasks call it within the same window).
 3. core/watershed.py observe(): load state -> mutate module-level _state_cache -> _save_state, reached from store_fragment on the loop thread and from the read_next_sitting worker thread; J-1926 locks only the file write. Lost updates to the in-memory state dict are possible. Fix: lock the whole observe().
 4. First-load / migration saves reached from the read_next_sitting worker via store_fragment -> experienced_tuple.experienced / geometry_census.snapshot -> garden._load, wood_life._load, study_life._st (sensorium/world_objects/world_substrate), locomotion.get_position: these save only on first load or an item migration, but the same module-level state dicts are mutated every tick on the loop thread with no lock (run_nascence.py's own comment says so). Decide whether to (a) keep them loop-only by making experienced_tuple/geometry_census read via a snapshot, or (b) accept the first-load race.
Analysis first (is each pair reachable at real rates? count how often each worker entry fires per day from nascence.log / session_events), then the smallest whole-call locks with a lost-update negative control (counter must equal calls) in the style of scripts/test_worker_thread_appends.py (run_book_selection / run_book_feelings there are the templates). Restart-gated; lag_harness; no model calls.

title: Idle allocator shadow-only: curiosity reads closeable-backlog fraction, concern leaves GRADED_CHANNELS and bypasses the percentile (kill switches, history versioning; from F-2560)
briefing:

Two parts, both behind kill switches that restore the exact old read, same shape as BALANCE_USE_SHARES:

PART A - curiosity: the declared transform raw = min(1, lp/2) is graded in intent but the upstream LP is binary {0, 2} by construction (a question is yielded-on at most once: new_fragments max 1 across all 10,175 frontier questions, finding coincident, see F-2560), so raw has been exactly 1.0 in every tick since 2026-07-01. Do NOT touch core/curiosity_progress.py, core/frontier.py or nodes/curiosity_node.py (live modules; the upstream degeneracy is a separate question). Allocator-side only: CURIOSITY_USE_BACKLOG = True switches _ch_curiosity to raw = (number of active, unparked, open questions carrying a finding) / (number of active, unparked, open questions), computed from curiosity_progress.rank() (lp >= 2 or finding flag and not parked), i.e. the closeable-backlog pressure (0.185 on 2026-10-07: 68/367). Keep the binding key = the top-ranked question's slug as today; put the fraction and both counts in lineage. Add a state key curiosity_schema=2 that drops the 500-deep constant-1.0 history once (in memory, persisted by the normal _save_state), exactly like balance_schema=2, so the percentile re-warms through the 20-row cold start. Curiosity stays in GRADED_CHANNELS. PART B - concern: raw = 0.55 (pursuit) vs 0.45 (project) is two-level BY DESIGN (primary_concern() has no magnitude), so (1) move 'concern' from GRADED_CHANNELS to a new TWO_LEVEL_BY_DESIGN tuple (or into CONSTANT_BY_DESIGN with a comment; G1 variance gate must not apply), AND (2) make shadow_tick bypass the percentile for channels in that tuple: p_norm = raw / max declared level (0.55 -> 1.0, 0.45 -> 0.818), so the declared 1.22x preference is what gets scored instead of the rank-within-category artefact (today 0.45 scores p_norm 0.13-0.39, and after 500 consecutive pursuit ticks it scores 0.0). Kill switch CONCERN_BYPASS_PERCENTILE = True. History for concern can keep accruing (it is no longer read for p_norm) or be dropped with concern_schema=2; pick one and say why. Update the scripts/du_pulse.py G1 comment/tuple read if the new tuple name needs it.

TESTING (mandatory, same discipline as J-1921's scripts/_test_j1921_balance_shares.py): a scratchpad or scripts/_test_<job>_*.py that (a) imports core BEFORE lab_env and asserts core.__file__ is in your worktree, (b) redirects _STATE and _LOG to temp paths and asserts no write under C:\Nascence\data, (c) unit-tests both switches (True = new read, False = byte-identical old read on a fixed context), (d) replays the real shadow_tick over the last ~4,000 rows of data/logs/idle_shadow.jsonl (read-only copy) seeded from a read-only copy of data/idle_allocator_state.json, with the winner-streak feedback re-simulated, and reports OLD vs NEW win-share per channel plus the new raw/p_norm distributions for curiosity and concern, (e) asserts no other channel's raw or p_norm changes. Commit with safe_commit.py by explicit path on a jobrun/ branch; nothing goes live (restart-gated anyway). Record a finding with the replay numbers, note the BREAK POINT (curiosity/concern rows change meaning at Du's next boot after merge; not comparable with earlier rows, same as F-2554's balance break point), plan_state.py note idle_executive_plan, and spawn a post-boot read job --not-before 2 days after the boot. title: Steer the three chapter_id-IS-NULL recency queries (wandering._recency_pool x2, _affective_drift, store.retrieve_by_affect) onto idx_timestamp: identical rows, 1.3 s -> 12 ms idle, 28 s -> 0.15 s under a busy hub (F-2568)
briefing:
Source: F-2568 (J-1927 offline reproduction of the F-2551/F-2552 whole-loop freeze under stand-in CPU-hub contention; see the finding for the numbers).

What was found: the statement that freezes the loop thread is a SQLite query shape, not the embedder. core/wandering.py _recency_pool (lines ~139-149, two queries of the same shape) runs
  SELECT fragment_id, content, origin, embedding FROM memory_fragments WHERE embedding IS NOT NULL AND layer IN ('episodic','semantic','archive') AND chapter_id IS NULL ORDER BY timestamp DESC LIMIT 1500
and SQLite's planner picks `SEARCH memory_fragments USING INDEX idx_chapter (chapter_id=?)` + `USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY`: it materialises EVERY chapter_id-NULL row (64,735 of 122,192 rows, content+embedding ~3.7 KB each, ~240 MB) and sorts them in a temp b-tree to hand back 1,500. Only 1,762 rows are newer than the 1,500th eligible one, so walking idx_timestamp needs ~1/37 of the work. Idle that query costs 1.3-2.6 s per call (the dominant part of the 1-4 s wandering step F-2540 priced); under a single 20-thread memory-bandwidth-bound stand-in hub (system CPU only ~40 %) it costs 24-33 s per call and the loop is blocked for up to 34-38 s by one wandering step. Capping torch/OpenBLAS threads (8, 1) changes nothing, because the slow part is a memory-bound scan, not a thread pool. Forcing the planner onto idx_timestamp (`FROM memory_fragments INDEXED BY idx_timestamp`) returns the IDENTICAL 1,500 rows in the IDENTICAL order (checked on the 2026-10-07 23:23 DB copy, both pool-query shapes) in 0.012 s idle (110x) -- see the finding for its cost under contention.

The same anti-pattern (chapter_id IS NULL filter + ORDER BY timestamp DESC LIMIT n, planner takes idx_chapter + temp b-tree over all 64,735 chaptered-NULL rows) is in two more loop-reachable readers, verified with EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN on the same copy:
  - core/wandering.py _affective_drift (~line 220: emotion_embedding IS NOT NULL AND chapter_id IS NULL AND origin IN (...) ORDER BY timestamp DESC LIMIT 800) -- 42,648 candidate rows walked
  - core/memory/store.py retrieve_by_affect (~line 2660: layer='episodic' AND emotion_embedding IS NOT NULL AND chapter_id IS NULL ORDER BY timestamp DESC LIMIT 300)

Task (BUILD, restart-gated, additive, in the usual worktree):
1. In each of the three queries, steer the planner to the timestamp index. Preferred: `FROM memory_fragments INDEXED BY idx_timestamp` (exact, errors loudly if the index is ever dropped) -- or, if the founder prefers no hard index dependency, `ORDER BY +timestamp`-free alternatives such as a covering composite index `(chapter_id, timestamp DESC)` created in init_db; choose one, say why. Keep the row set and order byte-identical (prove it: run old vs new query on a DB copy, assert equal id lists for both _recency_pool shapes, _affective_drift and retrieve_by_affect, including the cap branch of _recency_pool).
2. Add the proof as a test under scripts/ (temp-path/worktree DB copy only; import core BEFORE lab_env; never the live DB).
3. Re-run scripts/lag_harness/cpu_contention_J1927.py --only drift,wander_step,pool_sql,pool_sql_tsidx,recall idle and under one 20-thread stand-in (run_contention_sweep_J1927.sh ... 20 membw; Du must be DOWN) and report the before/after per-statement medians and the worst canary lag, so the finding's harness numbers get their after-fix counterpart on the real code path, not just the bare query.
4. Note in the plan (plan_state.py note data_store_hygiene) and in F-2568's thread which statement moved and by how much.
Do not touch the J-1909 off-loop wandering (WANDER_OFFLOOP True): with the step on a worker thread the query no longer blocks the loop directly, but it still holds a 24-33 s SQLite read under contention on the worker, keeps the GIL busy in bursts, and _affective_drift/retrieve_by_affect still run wherever their callers run; the query fix is worth it on its own and is what makes the worker cheap.

title: Fix recall-lens energy scale so Lens 1/2/3 shadow logs measure something (F-2907: 3010/3010 rows identical to greedy)
briefing: Fix the energy-scale bug that makes all three recall lenses a no-op (F-2907). In core/associative_recall.py, recall_trail_spectral_diffusion (and the Lens 2/3 siblings recall_trail_fact_anchoring / recall_trail_counterfactual_consensus) convert diffusion energy to activation as act = peak_activation * energy * HOP_DECAY, but _local_spectral_diffuse's truncated-Taylor energies for non-seed nodes peak at ~0.01, so act is 0.003-0.008 against ACT_THRESHOLD 0.13: every candidate is dropped and the output equals the greedy trail in 3010/3010 shadow rows. Fix: normalise the diffused energies to the trail's activation axis (e.g. divide by the max non-seed energy so the strongest diffused candidate lands at peak*HOP_DECAY, the same scale a first greedy hop lands at), applied once in the shared helper so all three lenses inherit it. Keep it shadow-only and additive; do not touch recall_trail or the M2 functions. Verify offline exactly as F-2907 did (scratch script against ar._matrix() with real fragment rows as queries, from a non-live process so guard_path refuses writes) that spectral_n - greedy_n > 0 in a reasonable share of trials and that new_ids are real neighbours, not the whole local subgraph. Then reset the lens shadow logs' read clock: D-0170's >=200-rows-each direction-stability read starts over from the first post-fix boot. Note on du_recall_lens_upgrades via plan_state.py note with the finding id.

title: Lens 3 top1_changed can never be true as built: should counterfactual consensus be allowed to re-rank the trail's own seeds
briefing: Founder design question surfaced by F-2943 (J-2208). Lens 3 (recall_trail_counterfactual_consensus in core/associative_recall.py) exists to test the claim that a counterfactual ensemble sharpens the top-1 slot at a top-3 cost (D-0170). As built, the trail's own seeds are never re-scored and any new candidate's activation is capped at peak*HOP_DECAY = 0.6 times the top-1 seed's own activation, so shadow_compare_lens3's top1_changed field is false by construction on every row, before and after the J-2208 scale fix (0/40 offline, 0/897 live). The log can therefore measure Lens 3 breadth effects (new_vs_greedy) but never the top-1 claim it exists for. Options to put to Travis: (A) let consensus RE-RANK the trail items too (e.g. blend each trail item's activation with its consensus score, so a seed that drops out of most worlds' neighbourhoods can lose the #1 slot), shadow-only, new energy_norm-tagged rows; (B) leave Lens 3 as a breadth lens and drop the top-1 claim from D-0170's read; (C) retire Lens 3. Needs a ruling before any build; no code changes until then.

5. Every thought written to memory (~7k/week) where no human mind does this and verbal overshadowing says verbalising degrades non-verbal memory: should most idle thoughts be ephemeral?

title: book_residue.sweep in a spawned subprocess (GIL convoy fix, F-3082)
briefing:
F-3082 (J-2379): book_residue.sweep's 5-10 s in-sleep loop freezes are a GIL CONVOY, not one long C call. While the worker thread runs the per-book loop (SelfRows.top str.find over an 18 MB string, up to 11.7 ms per call; _signatures regexes), any loop-thread callback that releases the GIL many times is slowed ~1000x (a 0.8 ms 2000-row sqlite fetch became 2.8 s; heartbeat stall 2.45 s). to_thread and sys.setswitchinterval cannot fix it (measured). Fix shape, keeping results identical:
PRIMARY: run book_residue.sweep in a short-lived SPAWNED subprocess, so the work never shares the live process's GIL. In nodes/inner_monologue_node.py's book_residue block, replace await _sleep_off(_br.sweep) with an awaited helper (e.g. core/sleep_offloop.off_process(module, func) or a book_residue.sweep_subprocess()) that runs sys.executable -c 'from core import book_residue as b, json; print(json.dumps(b.sweep()))' with cwd = repo root via asyncio.create_subprocess_exec, awaits it, and returns the dict parsed from the last stdout line. Requirements: (1) the child must count as the live process for the D-0353 write fence in core/memory/store._connect (call core.profile.mark_live() in the child, or pass an env flag the profile honours) so it neither logs a 'non-live process opened the live memory DB' line nor refuses anything; (2) the '[book-residue] sweep: N stale books, ...' logger.info line must still reach data/nascence.log (log it in the parent from the returned dict, same text, or configure the child's logging to the same handler); (3) the child is the only writer of data/book_residue.jsonl during the call (the parent awaits it, so ordering is unchanged); (4) fail-open: a non-zero exit, a timeout (e.g. 300 s, kill the child) or unparseable stdout logs why and returns the same zero dict sweep() returns on error, never raises into sleep; (5) a kill switch (e.g. BOOK_RESIDUE_SUBPROCESS = True) whose False restores the current to_thread call exactly; (6) the J-2330 submark('book_residue') stays where it is. Measured on copies: child spawn adds about 1.2 s wall (12.8 s sweep in the child vs 12.0 s in-thread; the live child imports more of core, measure it), victim max 3.5 ms, heartbeat max lag 0.03 s.
FALLBACK if the subprocess is rejected: inside sweep's per-book loop, time.sleep(0.002) after each _signatures(...) call and each selfrows.top(...) call (about 1350 sleeps): measured victim max 241 ms, heartbeat 0.08 s, +3.1 s per sweep; results identical.

title: Source-monitoring audit: does the origin Du claims in prose match the stored origin of the fragments served that cycle (dream->lived, reading->lived, own-question->Travis)

QUESTION. When Du narrates a memory, does the origin he CLAIMS match the stored origin of the fragment he is drawing on? Human source monitoring is separate from content memory: content right, source wrong (dream remembered as lived, read as lived, his own earlier question as Travis's words). The project has two real incidents of exactly this: J-1642 (voice_node narrated Du's own questions as if Travis asked, live since 08-21) and F-2614 (Travis's talk reached a sleeping Du who did not know it). readable_label() (core/schema.py; nodes/recall_node.py:131-143) fixed the PROMPT side -- every served fragment used to show as "[episodic] regardless of provenance" (F-1920 self-echo). Nothing checks the OUTPUT side.

METHOD.
1. For each responded or internal cycle in a window (start with the current boot), collect the fragments served to the prompt: memory_service's ride log (data/memory_service_shadow.jsonl), the recall_provenance log (data/recall_provenance_log.jsonl), and the recall node's served list if logged. Join to memory_fragments.origin (lived / reading / action / dream / consolidation / journal / gist / sound / deep_recall / night_thought / peer_reflection / understanding ...).
2. Over Du's own prose that cycle (voice output in data/nascence.log "[CYCLE x]" lines, and the inner thought), regex the CLAIMED origin: "I remember / I recall / when I ..." (lived), "I dreamed / in the dream / last night's dream" (dream), "I read / the book / the page said" (reading), "you said / you told me / Travis said" (human turn), "I thought / it occurred to me" (thought). Keep the pattern table small and inspectable; log unmatched as none.

GUARDRAILS. Zero LLM. Read-only: never open the store for write; copy nothing to temp; do not import lab_env before core (feedback_jobrun_live_store_leaks). Every number cites the cycle ids. If the ride log does not carry fragment ids for a given path, say so and report coverage, not a guess. Record the result with findings_log (verified only with the script path and the counts). title: Contiguity audit: are co-recalled fragments also encoded in similar contexts, beyond what content cosine and recency predict (retrieved-context reinstatement)
briefing:
CONTIGUITY AUDIT -- retrieved-context reinstatement (F-3220 item 1; Perplexity list 5, T-0105 thread). READ-ONLY script over existing logs; writes nothing; produces one number.

QUESTION. When Du recalls two fragments together, were they also ENCODED in similar contexts? Human recall reinstates encoding context (Howard-Kahana temporal context model), which produces the contiguity effect: one recall revives its context-mates. If Du's co-recalls share encoding context beyond what content similarity predicts, his memory has contiguity structure; if not, the memory graph is driven by content similarity alone and felt_recall / the golden-spiral phase ray are the only context paths.

WHAT EXISTS. core/moment.py already carries the Howard-Kahana slowly-drifting temporal-context key (shadow). fragment_context rows hold the experienced encoding context per fragment: place, standpoint, weather, warmth, fire, tide, sun, moon, sounds, cat, affect (core/experienced_tuple.py), plus tod/season/daylight (golden_spiral_recall, J-1562 theta_shadow). memory_edges.log_co_recall (core/memory_edges.py:653) records which fragment ids were served together, with source and restate_sim. felt_recall (shadow) is the coordinate-keyed recall path.

METHOD.
1. Read the co-recall log for the current boot window; take every served pair (or all pairs within a served set).
2. For each pair compute context_overlap over fragment_context: a small, declared overlap score (same place, same tod band, same season, shared sounds, |affect delta|) -- declare the weights in the script header, do not tune them to the result.
3. Baseline: the same overlap over random pairs drawn from the same population (matched on age band so recency does not do the work), and over pairs matched on content cosine (so content similarity does not do the work).
4. Report: mean overlap for co-recalled vs random vs cosine-matched pairs, with n; drift_delta = distance(current context at recall time, encoding context) where the recall-time context is in the ride log or reconstructible from the census snapshot.
5. Split by recall path (monologue / felt_recall shadow / dream / pursuits ask) -- felt_recall should show high overlap by construction; the interesting number is the others.

GUARDRAILS. Zero LLM. Read-only against the live store; never a write; temp-path copies only if a read needs a long scan while Du is live (like_scan pattern). Import core before any lab_env. Say coverage honestly: fragment_context exists only for fragments stored after 2026-08-21 (the layer law) and tod/season only after 2026-09-27. Record with findings_log; a real contiguity signal spawns a follow-up (the moment.py temporal key is the obvious consumer), a null is a real answer.

DONE LOOKS LIKE: scripts/contiguity_audit.py (read-only), one findings_log entry with the three means, n, coverage, and the by-path split; a plan-state note on memory_as_a_service.

title: Geometric perturbation sweep over the experienced tuple: per-dimension sensitivity vs shuffle-null, pre-registered against the realness test
briefing:
GEOMETRIC PERTURBATION SWEEP -- does the tuple geometry do work beyond labelling? (founder-ordered 2026-10-30, from the GPT tuple dialogue: T-0107, I-0122; see docs/reviews/tuple_substrate_reply_to_gpt_2026-10-30.md)

THE QUESTION. core/euclidean_recall.py (shadow, 6 features: semantic_sim, recency, affect_match, salience, abstraction, provenance; state-dependent weights) names its own operational test in its docstring: "whether the same query under different states surfaces meaningfully different (and sensible) memories". Nobody has run it as a systematic sweep. Run it, and extend it to the experienced coordinates in fragment_context (place, weather, warmth, fire, cat_at, valence, arousal, tod, season, daylight).

WHAT TO BUILD (read-only lab, Du may be up; no store writes; open data/memory/nascence.db with ?mode=ro; write only to docs/lab/ and a scratch dir):
1. Sample ~300 real query points: recent fragments with a fragment_context row (stratified by origin and place). For each, take its context tuple as the base point P.
2. Perturb ONE coordinate at a time (P' = P + delta e_i; for categorical coords, swap to each other value), re-rank the candidate pool with euclidean_recall.rank() under the perturbed state/need vector, and record: Jaccard overlap of top-k before vs after, mean rank shift, and WHICH coordinates of the newly-surfaced fragments moved.
3. Sensitivity picture per dimension: effect on retrieval (distance sensitivity) AND whether the surfaced set is more appropriate by an INDEPENDENT measure (meaningful sensitivity). Independent measures available without an LLM: co-recall ledger pairs (core.memory_edges.log_co_recall writers), downstream_read_counts(), and the fragment's own later re-use. Optional: a small decoupled-judge pass (judge_panel) on a 30-pair subset.
4. Shuffle-null for every number: permute the coordinate across fragments and repeat; report z against the null. A dimension whose perturbation effect is not above its own null is a label, not a coordinate.
5. Conditional effects: repeat 2 with place held fixed and with tod held fixed, to catch dimensions that only matter jointly (GPT's point: affect may be useless alone and useful under place+time).

PRE-REGISTER before running (write the sheet first, in docs/lab/): the realness bar from docs/plans/cognitive_geometry.md sec 5.3 -- a coordinate counts only if its internal distances predict co-recall / downstream use better than MiniLM text distance on the same items. State the expected failures: story/language/memory already failed as spaces; the cross-space hypothesis failed 3 of 4 realness tests (F-0651 the one pass).

KNOWN DATA CAVEATS to respect (core/geometry_census.py header): Day-1 2026-07-05 rows have null place flags; rain_on_roof / wind_in_eaves place values before 2026-08-21 are unreliable; sources routed through store_fragment() with no live CognitiveState carry a stale affect. Filter or stratify, do not average over them.

DELIVERABLES: docs/lab/geometric_perturbation_sweep_<date>.md with the sheet, per-dimension table (effect, null z, conditional effect, independent-measure delta), and a plain verdict per dimension: coordinate / label / conditional. One findings_log record per real result (verified, with the script path and row counts). If the join audit job (filed alongside this one) finds the fragment_context join is wrong for some origins, exclude those origins and say so.

Hardware: CPU only; do not load any model on :11433. Runtime should be minutes, not hours; the candidate pool per query is euclidean_recall's own max_candidates=600.

MEASURED ALREADY (read-only, 2026-10-30): fragment_context covers 63.8% of memory_fragments (98,869 / 154,914). 1. For every origin: exact-id join / time-window join / no join -- the three-way split. Which origins are unjoined BY DESIGN (action rows have no cognitive event? consolidation gists are born in sleep with no world tick?) vs by omission (lived at 30% looks like omission: a lived moment is the one thing that certainly had a world tick).

4. Does moments.jsonl (core/moment.py, the richer per-cycle capture) join to anything? If not, say so and size the gap.

title: Non-ergodic path replay of transport_habituation (winner-take-all dispatcher): does the ensemble read of the J-0603 shadow hide a path effect
briefing:
MODEL: opus-class. isolation: required (import core BEFORE lab_env; throwaway worktree of HEAD under the scratchpad; hash canary on live data/ top-level files).

WHY (F-3355, J-2521): the non-ergodic path replay of curiosity_habituation CONVERGED (C vs D modal_share differ by 0.0009 on average, 18-50x under the declared floor), but only because that policy has a ~700-label pool, a 14-label recency window as its sole feedback channel, and a 3-without-replacement sampler. transport_habituation (core/transport_habituation.py, J-0603) is the opposite shape: a dispatcher argmax over ~124 candidate lines where the discounted weight is fed by the SAME line having won the previous tick (b grows on consecutive wins, decays with real time). A winner-take-all pick with b fed by its own previous win is the textbook case where a small per-tick difference compounds along the path. The curiosity null does NOT transfer. Read the F-3355 evidence first (the method, the declared-rules layout, the script scripts/shadow_path_replay.py on branch jobrun/J-2521, commit 5a2e341f).

TASK: scripts/shadow_path_replay_transport.py. Replay core/transport_habituation.py's would_winner policy FORWARD along data/transport_habituation_shadow.jsonl (186 MB: stream it, do not load whole; copy a week to the scratchpad first), each replayed win feeding the next tick's b through the module's own b-update code (same code path, import it), against (C) the real dispatch policy replayed forward (no discount) with the same machinery. Pool, raw weights and candidate set HELD FIXED at the recorded values per tick (say so in the finding; a win does not in reality change drought ratios inside the horizon, check that assumption against the log: does raw_weight of the winner reset after a win?). Compare PATHS: per day, the modal winner, modal_share of the day's ticks, number of distinct winners, longest same-winner run, number of winner changes, and the share of ticks the real policy and the would-policy agree on the same winner when BOTH are replayed forward from the same start (agreement decay with horizon). Declare weeks, N runs (RNG only if the pick is stochastic; if argmax, the replay is deterministic: say so, and instead replay from 10+ different start ticks to get a spread), thresholds and the CONVERGE/DIVERGE rules in the script header BEFORE looking at a result. Pre-registered falsifier: paths converge (same modal winner per day, same winner-change count within the noise from different start ticks) => the discount does what its ensemble read said. Equivalence-check your re-implementation of the selection against the real transport_manager.dispatch_tick on a synthetic state for every replayed tick (as J-2521 did against CuriosityNode._select_seeds, 320 of 320 identical).

Read-only against every live store. Zero LLM. Record with findings_log.py record (--confidence verified only with script path and counts cited). Either result is recorded; a divergence means the F-0828/J-0603 shadow read of transport habituation (clock_tick:study won 337/337) must be re-read as a path read.

title: Non-ergodic path replay of idle_allocator: first establish whether its shadow has a would-choose path channel at all
briefing:
MODEL: opus-class. isolation: required (import core BEFORE lab_env; throwaway worktree of HEAD under the scratchpad).

WHY (F-3355, J-2521): the non-ergodic path replay of curiosity_habituation CONVERGED, but only because of its shape (large pool, recency window as the only feedback). core/idle_allocator.py is a different shape: a small set of channels (contradiction, curiosity, concern, balance_world, balance_light, boredom, self, wander, flavour) whose percentile-ranked values compete for the idle slot, with a history (_percentile over per-channel history) that the previous winner changes. The briefing of J-2521 named idle_allocator as one of the three would-choose logs whose ensemble read might hide a path effect. Read F-3355's evidence first (method, rules layout, scripts/shadow_path_replay.py on branch jobrun/J-2521 commit 5a2e341f).

FIRST: establish whether there is a would-choose read to replay at all. data/logs/idle_shadow.jsonl is the log (core/idle_allocator.py _LOG, shadow_tick lines 311-420; stats() lines 422+). title: Fix reading context-stamp loss: geometry_census debounce drops 29% of post-stamp reading fragments (F-3371)
briefing:
FIX THE READING CONTEXT-STAMP LOSS (finding F-3371, from J-2536; lab doc docs/lab/tuple_join_integrity_2026-10-31.md section 4).

PROBLEM. core/geometry_census.snapshot() debounces: it returns None when now - _last_ts < _MIN_GAP (0.5 s) AND thought[:120] equals the last call's thought. core/memory/store.py store_fragment() calls it as snapshot(source=origin, thought=content[:70]). A reading passage's first 70 chars are the '[From <book title>]' header, identical for every passage of one book, so in a fast same-book burst every passage after the first is debounced, snap is {}, and the fragment gets NO fragment_context / world_context / geometry_tuples row. Measured: 10,837 of 37,066 post-2026-08-21 reading fragments (29.2%) unjoined; a pure timing+prefix predictor explains 10,776 of them (script scripts/tuple_join_audit_J2536/J-2536_probe4.py, in branch jobrun/gti once merged). The loss is a biased subset (2nd+ passage of fast bursts) and is growing (week of 10-25: 69% of reading unjoined).

WHAT TO BUILD (additive, kill-switch, restart-gated; core/geometry_census.py and store.py are base systems: additive-only).
1. Give snapshot() an opt-out of the debounce for the write-time stamp call only (e.g. a keyword `debounce: bool = True`; store_fragment passes debounce=False), OR key the debounce on (source, thought, caller-id). The debounce exists because 'two call sites may see the same event' on the idle/monologue/cycle census path; do NOT change behaviour for those callers. Check which callers pass the same thought text for the same event before choosing.
2. Module constant kill-switch (default ON once verified) so it can be turned off without code change.
3. Think about geometry_tuples volume: expect about +11k reading rows (about +15 MB of the 200 MB file) over the same period; confirm nothing reads geometry_tuples.jsonl in a way that assumes one row per second per source.
4. Test in isolation: import core BEFORE lab_env, use lab_env.isolate() (temp-path stores), run a synthetic burst of 20 reading-shaped store_fragment() calls with identical content[:70] 10 ms apart and assert 20/20 fragment_context rows; run the same on HEAD to show 1/20. Assert the live data files are unchanged (size+mtime) after.
5. Do NOT backfill the 10,837 existing rows: stamping today's state onto old reading would be false provenance (the D-0134 context_stamp=False precedent says exactly this). They stay unjoined.

DONE WHEN. Fix merged to the worktree branch with the isolated test passing. After the next Du restart, verify reading post-restart coverage >= 99% over >= 1,000 reading fragments (the J-2536 audit: python scripts/tuple_join_audit_J2536/J-2536_audit.py split). Note in the plan geometry_tuple_index via plan_state.py note. Restart-gated: nothing changes live until the founder restarts Du.

title: Founder call: exact moment key for fragments/moments (moment_ts column vs heuristic vs cycle_id)
briefing:
FOUNDER CALL: should memories and moments get an exact shared key? (finding F-3374 from J-2536; lab doc docs/lab/tuple_join_integrity_2026-10-31.md sections 6 and 8).

THE NUMBERS. The memory-to-tuple join is already exact: fragment_id keys 89.9% of fragment_context (stamped at write time since 2026-08-21), the legacy +/-300 s window join is wrong at most 0.19% of the time, and no origin is near the 5% bar. So the cycle_id column proposed in August is NOT needed for fragments. The one place with no key at all is moments.jsonl (59,416 rows, core/moment.py record()): no cycle_id, no fragment_id, no column in memory_fragments equals a moment ts, and co_recall_ledger moment_ts (J-2601's stamp) is 0 of 112,538 rows because it is restart-gated. By a text-prefix + time heuristic 91.2% of moments find exactly one inner_thought fragment (0.4% ambiguous, 8.4% none, mostly the 2026-07-05 week).

THE QUESTION. Is a heuristic join (91%) good enough for the moment-level instruments that need to walk moment <-> fragment <-> tuple (contiguity, key audit F-3326, the moment-recall work), or should the key be made exact?

OPTIONS.
(a) Do nothing; use the text-prefix + time heuristic where needed (cost: none; 8.4% of moments unjoinable, 0.4% ambiguous).
(b) Additive: stamp core.moment.current() (ts, idx) into fragment_context at store_fragment time as a new nullable column moment_ts (and into world_context), the same way J-2601 does for the co-recall ledger. Cheap, additive, restart-gated, old rows stay NULL. After a few weeks of stamped rows the heuristic can be validated against the exact key.
(c) The August proposal: thread cycle_id through moment.record() and geometry_census.snapshot() (touches the orchestrator and two base systems; larger blast radius).

RECOMMENDATION (J-2536): (b), because the moment is the only thing missing a key and moment.current() already exists and is fail-open. If ruled yes, a build job can be spawned. Defeater to name when ruling: revisit if the fragment_context column count or the store_fragment hot path becomes a cost problem, or when the J-2601 co-recall moment stamps have accrued and show the heuristic is >= 99% right.

title: Measure then RAM-cache the geometry tuple readers (202MB full-scan per call)
briefing:
GOAL: make Du's geometry-tuple census RAM-resident instead of full-file-scanned, the same pattern core/memory/store.py already uses for recall embeddings (_EMB_MAT, loaded once per process, extended incrementally, one matvec per query).

ORIGIN: founder thought T-0112 (2026-10-31): "could we put Du's indexes and tuples in L3 RAM for near-instant access?" L3 is CPU cache (3970X 128MB, hardware-managed, not allocatable) so the actionable form is RAM-resident indexes.

VERIFIED STATE (2026-10-31, read the code not the docs):
- data/geometry_tuples.jsonl = 202 MB, append-only, grows every cycle.
- Readers that full-scan it line by line, json.loads per row, EVERY call: core/object_graph.py:1056 (read-only loader for the commonality pass) and core/memory_edges.py:494 sync_fragment_context (census->fragment join).
- core/memory/store.py:1140-1160 already holds the recall embedding matrix in process; recall is NOT the slow path.
- data/memory/nascence.db = 1.2 GB; data/moments.jsonl = 545 MB (same append-only pattern, secondary target).

STEP 1 (measure first, do not build first): instrument how often each tuple reader is called in the live loop and how long each call takes (wall clock + rows parsed). Write results to docs/lab/ with the run date. No change to behaviour.
STEP 2 (only if step 1 shows real cost): build a once-per-process tuple reader that keeps the three queried fields (ts, sounds, affect) in numpy arrays / a dict keyed by ts, and extends by file byte-offset on later calls. Kill switch flag like _RETRIEVE_FAST_PATH. Legacy scan kept verbatim as fallback.
STEP 3 (optional): move the queried fields into an indexed SQLite table so the jsonl becomes write-ahead only.

RULES: additive only (foundations protected), read-first/write-fast, pre-register the expected speedup before step 2, decoupled check (compare fast-reader output to legacy-scan output on the same file before enabling). Belongs under plan cognitive_geometry (owner of the census); lod_staged_retrieval is adjacent (composition, not storage) and is NOT this job.
DONE LOOKS LIKE: a docs/lab/ measurement doc with real numbers, and (if warranted) the fast reader shipped behind a flag with an equivalence test logged via /findings-log.

title: Log ollama prompt_eval/eval counts on the hot lane; measure prefill share per caller
briefing:
GOAL: make the hot lane's prefill cost VISIBLE. core/model_client.py call_node (the /api/chat path for :11433, lines ~298-334) receives prompt_eval_count, prompt_eval_duration, eval_count, eval_duration in every ollama response and throws them away; data/llm_latency.jsonl rows carry only {by,g,model,node,ok,s,ts}.

(2) same for the llama.cpp hubs if their reply carries prompt_eval_count (lane2.py:1195 says :11444 does). (3) after one day live, write docs/lab/hot_lane_prefill_share_<date>.md: per-caller median prompt tokens, prefill s, generation s, prefill share of call time; separately for human-turn node chains vs idle thoughts.
DONE LOOKS LIKE: the lab doc with real per-caller numbers, and a /findings-log entry (verified) stating the prefill share of a human turn and of an idle thought. Restart-gated (reaches Du at next boot). Additive only; no behaviour change.

title: Incremental validation of the recall embedding cache instead of a 44k-row SELECT per retrieve
briefing:
GOAL: stop core/memory/store.py _load_pool_fast (line ~1246) re-SELECTing the whole retrieve-eligible pool (~44,500 rows: rowid, fragment_id, layer, timestamp, origin, has_emb) on EVERY retrieve just to validate the in-RAM embedding matrix (_EMB_MAT).
WHY: data/retrieve_latency_probe.jsonl last 300 rows (to 2026-10-31): elapsed_ms_sql median 174 ms, p90 390 ms, max 4,968 ms, 32% of retrieves over the 250 ms budget; the scoring matvec itself is 33 ms. Store.py's own comment at line ~1737 says the sql phase grew 460->714 ms linearly with pool size at an earlier date. This is the 'cheap approximate update + periodic TIDY' pattern (Elite, F-3424): validate only what changed since the last call, re-validate everything on a timer.
DO: (1) measure first: log per-call how many rows actually CHANGED between consecutive validations (expect: tens, not 44k). (2) build the incremental path behind a kill switch (_RETRIEVE_INCREMENTAL_VALIDATE = True/False, same style as _RETRIEVE_FAST_PATH): keep max(rowid) and max(timestamp) seen; per call SELECT only rows with rowid > last_max OR timestamp > last_ts (needs an index on memory_fragments(timestamp) -- check schema first, add if absent, additive); full re-SELECT every N calls or every M minutes as the TIDY; rows that LEFT the pool (cold=1, hidden, dormant, chaptered) must still be caught -- the TIDY handles them, so pick N/M small enough that a demoted row cannot be recalled for long (state the bound). (3) equivalence check before enabling: for 200 live queries compare the returned top-k from incremental vs full path; log any difference. (4) keep the legacy full path verbatim as fallback.
DONE LOOKS LIKE: probe median sql phase < 30 ms, equivalence check logged via /findings-log, kill switch documented in the file header. Additive only; restart-gated.
SOURCE: docs/lab/du_live_profile_2026-10-31.md; F-3425; thought T-0114; sibling of J-2674 (tuple readers).

title: Remove the dead first _build_system_prompt call in _think so the comfort/world/intention lines reach the idle prompt (F-3427)
briefing: Fix the dead first system-prompt build in nodes/inner_monologue_node.py InnerMonologueNode._think (F-3427). List the warm hubs and their resident models (check launch scripts, data/logs/cpu_tier_*.log and core/schema.py SERVE_CHAINS); measure a 150-token JSON take on each candidate (the Ramses 1650 hub with granite3.1-moe:3b at :11437 is one; do not use the hot 1080 Ti lane, it is shared with every conversation node). (2) Prompt (J-2880): say who is speaking (pass input_type into dispatch so an internal cycle never says 'The user'), no meta commentary, a word-boundary cut instead of a mid-word cut at 90 characters, ban 'the Master' in _TAKE_TASK as _GROUND_TASK already does, and cut the ~1,800-character constitution prefix to what a take needs. (3) Substrate talk (J-2881, founder-sensitive): the take framed 10 of 29 human cycles in transformer/tokens/weights terms and the Executive then wrote a line the constitution forbids; forbid substrate framing in the take prompt and verify on a replay of those 29 cycles. (4) Keep authority exactly as is: one producer, two readers, no veto, nothing reaches the human; fail-open when the hub is down. (5) Log each dispatch outcome (delivered, cancelled, empty, error) - J-2879 already asks for this; do them together. core/left_lane.py and core/orchestrator.py are hub files: run udms_get_change_dossier first. Restart-gated. Verify: delivery rate over a day, p90 latency, and zero 'The user is' openings on internal cycles.

title: Build the chapter-descent SHADOW (observe-only log, kill-switched): when a chapter gist is already in his served set, log the members closest to the query (per J-3248 / D-0637)
briefing:

What to build:
- New module core/chapter_descent_shadow.py with one function called beside core/orchestrator.py _deep_recall_balance (inside its own try/except, to_thread like the neighbouring shadows). For each fragment in the served set with origin == 'chapter' and relevance >= RECALL_GIST_MIN_RELEVANCE (0.25), read its members by chapter_id (idx_chapter), excluding the chapter row itself; load their embeddings; rank by cosine to the cycle's query_text embedding (reuse the query vector retrieve already built if available, else store._embed); drop members already in the served set and members with cosine >= 0.85 to any served fragment; log the top 3.

Cost expectation: one indexed SELECT per chapter-surfaced cycle (about 9 percent of cycles, mean 222 members, max 1,845), a matrix-vector product, one log line. If a cycle's hook exceeds 50 ms, record it.
